subsubtopic: RECORD RAINFALL IN LOWER MAINLAND OF BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that the 1937 record of 258 millimetres of rainfall has now been surpassed in the lower mainland of British Columbia by a new record of 331 millimetres, which has caused severe problems for farmers in the Fraser Valley, as many fruit and vegetable farmers are unable to plant their crops, while others are having seeds rot or wash away, and recognizing the $81 million paid to grain farmers, subsidies to the textile industry, etc., I move, seconded by the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon):
That the Minister of Agriculture take immediate action to ease the plight of the Fraser Valley farmers who face a minimum $15 million loss and are in a disaster situation because of the record amount of rainfall.

subsubtopic: CONDEMNATION OF LOWERING OF UNITED STATES CLEAN AIR STANDARDS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of very urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that the United States Environmental Protection Agency has defended recommendations that the U.S. Clean Air Act be weakened to such an extent that individual states will be able to compete for the lowest possible air quality standards in order to attract acid rain polluting industries, and in view of the fact that these proposals are a sellout of the environmental heritage of Canadians and American and fly in the face of work being done to achieve a clean air treaty between Canada and the United States, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
10830

June 22, 1981
That this House severely censure Anne Gorsuch, the U.S. EPA administrator, and strongly urge the Minister of the Environment to communicate the outrage of this House and all Canadians at the attempt to scuttle the work of the Canadian and U.S. governments in their attempt to reach a treaty on the limitation of long-range trans-boundary air pollutants.

subsubtopic: PETRO-CANADA'S ACQUISITION OF PETROFINA-CALL FOR JUDICIAL INQUIRY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to underscore allegations which have arisen from the purchase of Petrofina by the federal government. There is strong evidence of handsome windfall profits to insiders who may have benefited from advance information. There is a report that 91 senior employees of Petrofina netted over $10 million in profits through a company stock option plan. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) is on record as promising an internal investigation. This is tantamount to placing the cookie monster in charge of investigating missing cookies. This is far too serious a matter for a departmental or ministerial whitewash. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga):
That the Prime Minister act immediately to commence a judicial inquiry into the allegations that insiders profited from the sale of Petrofina to the Government of Canada, with the Canadian taxpayer picking up the tab.

THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. It concerns a letter which one of my constituents wrote him. It is a "Dear Allan" letter, asking for his suggestions on how Canadians should deal with inflation. My constituent, a single parent, asked the Minister of Finance:
Since I am now working at two jobs, seven days a week ... I would much appreciate your suggestions on how to tighten the belt that I cannot afford to buy.
She indicated that she buys her clothes at thrift stores, and that working seven days a week means there is not any recreation. She asked what other items she can do without, or how she can add some hours of work to earn a little more income.

When the owners of the apartment block in which I am living refinance their mortgage 1 expect my rent to go up quite significantly. Unless I can find some way to pay this increased rental, my daughter and I will have to leave the apartment, and believe me, in Vancouver there is no place to go.

CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Finance. On Saturday a young couple visited my office. In 1976 they bought an AHOP home with a 10 per cent CMHC mortgage. Financial assistance from the government brought the mortgage interest rate to 6 per cent. Last week CMHC graciously offered to renew the mortgage at 18 per cent. The monthly payments will leap from $174 per month to $444 per month. The minister has suggested that he has talked to the banks. I would ask him if he has talked to CMHC since it is the mortgagee in both cases. What does he expect a young couple to do without losing their home?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it was in direct response to situations such as the one the hon. member has specifically referred to that the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, with the assistance of the government last year, and again this year, introduced a program to protect people who might be faced with costs which were unreasonable, too high, or above the average which most Canadians are required to pay toward maintaining shelter needs.
In the case outlined by the hon. member, or in other cases where the amount of a person's income, or family income, required to meet shelter costs which go toward principal, interest and taxes that exceed 30 per cent of their income, the program provided for the government to continue its assistance
to those needy couples. I hope that the specific case mentioned by the hon. member will be brought to the attention of the local officials of CMHC, to see if they qualify for aid.

-some serious work is being done about changing the banking system in this country.
He also said:
-the government will change the banking system if the chartered banks don't do something to help farmers.
My question to the Minister of Finance is this: who speaks for the government in matters affecting the banks, interest rates and fiscal and monetary policy? Would the minister tell us if the government is seriously planning to change the banking system in this country? Would he tell us what it is the chartered banks are supposed to do to help farmers, particularly when the government's own bank is charging 21 per cent to 23 per cent on its loans? CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST INDIAN AND METIS WORKERS AT OCHRE RIVER, MAN.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question, in the absence of the Minister of Transport, is directed to the Minister of Labour. Considering the fact that a number of Indians and Metis in Manitoba are planning to blockade the CNR tracks outside Dauphin today because of alleged discrimination while working for the CNR, is the minister prepared to investigate independently the incident at
Oral Questions
Ochre River where 25 CNR extra-gang employees left their job due to discrimination?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST INDIAN AND METIS WORKERS AT OCHRE RIVER, MAN.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker,
I thank the hon. member for the question. I must quite honestly say to him, through Your Honour, that I am not aware of this incident, but that I certainly will make inquiries in relation to the department. The hon. member will quickly recognize that, if these are unionized employees, they have remedies under the collective agreement, and also of course under human rights. However, not having enough background,
I am unable to say to the hon. member at this moment that I would have a formal investigation made. What I would undertake is to make inquiries immediately into the situation, and based upon the facts, as they are ascertained, take whatever action is appropriate.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, these are extra-gang employees who would not be unionized. However, my supplementary question is for the same minister. Would the minister specifically address this issue of Indian harassment and the CNR's handling of this incident, with a mind to redressing the grievances that have been expressed?

subsubtopic: PROTECTION FOR MICMAC FISHERMEN ON RESTIGOUCHE RESERVE, P.Q.
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and it concerns the situation at Resti-gouche. The minister was asked on several occasions, as was the Prime Minister, to send aid to the Micmacs at the Resti-gouche reserve. He went down over the weekend and told them that he could not provide help to them in the form of protection, but that his very presence on the reserve offered protection. Now that he is not on the reserve, could he tell us what protection the Micmac Indians have at Restigouche at the present time?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: PROTECTION FOR MICMAC FISHERMEN ON RESTIGOUCHE RESERVE, P.Q.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not think the

Oral Questions
hon. member's preamble is very accurate. What I said is that I could not afford protection of the kind that I think some people, in their justifiably concerned state, were asking for, in terms of more alarms and talk about guns, tanks and so on. I do not believe that that was going to assist the situation in any possible way.
There is no question, though, that there is a good deal of fright permeating that entire community. I indicated that on my return here I would talk to my colleague, the Solicitor General, with respect to the return of the nets to the band. I have not had an opportunity to do so yet. Also, my officials had talks with the Quebec provincial police. They indicated that probably as of today they would be withdrawing the very heavy contingent of Quebec provincial police that are not on the reserve-they have not come on the reserve since June 11, but they are surrounding the reserve-that they would be withdrawing those people today. I am checking, and 1 am told that they have not been withdrawn yet. We are still hopeful that they will be withdrawn today.
As far as any further action that may be required is concerned, we are monitoring the situation each day. I had indicated that on my return I would be getting together with my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, to examine the nature of the application of the regulations under the Fisheries Act. June 22, 1981

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Has the minister had any discussion with the banks with regard to some credit allocation system to ensure that farmers, small businessmen and home owners are able to get their share of the credit supply without having to bid against the multinationals, business people making big takeovers, and the government, for that money supply?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the minister will know that large borrowings of over $ 1 million from the banking system are up 36 per cent this year, that a great deal of that borrowing has been to finance takeovers, and that today with inflation it is cheaper to buy an existing asset than to create new one. subtopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when I last spoke on this bill on June 17, I commented on the fact that the information we have with respect to corporate salaries and executive compensation in general is totally inadequate, indeed non-existent. It is not simply the Canadian

June 22, 1981
Corporations and Labour Unions
public who do not have access to this information, it is the shareholders of our largest corporations. This information is of direct concern not simply to the public and government, but also to shareholders of these companies.
We go through an annual ritual in this House, Madam Speaker, when the Securities and Exchange Commission in the United States releases certain information respecting executive compensation. That commission is required by law to release figures on executive compensation by companies subject to its jurisdiction. We as Canadians have access to that information, as any individual does, and so every year we get a glimpse of the extent of increases in that compensation and some idea as to what executives are being paid these days. The figures are indeed shocking. They show that for the last year the increases amounted to some 30 per cent on average; that the most senior executives in our largest companies are paid anywhere from $250,000 to $1 million a year in salary and benefits. We also discover that there is another class of benefits which is harder to measure but nevertheless has to be declared on the SEC form, that of deferred compensation and deferred benefits which excuse the executives from paying income tax.
We have these schemes in Canada and it was with respect to some of them that my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), was asking today: Well, why does not the government stop deferring this compensation, start collecting the taxes and provide benefits for those Canadians in need? The minister then went off on a tangent talking about the small business development bond and the banks, two totally unrelated subjects.
By the way, Mr. Speaker, the small business development bond has not existed long enough to have any effect on the rate of taxes paid by the banks. If he does not know and understand that, and know that the reason the banks are paying such a low level of tax has to do with the income debenture system which has been part of the Liberal system of taxation throughout the entire decade of the Trudeau government of 1968 to 1978, then he simply does not know some of the most elementary facts of taxation which are his responsibilities.
The hard fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that we do not have provision in this bill as it now stands to get the most basic and elementary kind of information on the question of who gets what, when, where and how in our society. We do not have equality of information because we are faced with the fact that salaries and benefits of Canadians of low and middle income are known. We know what welfare benefits are, we know what wages are because they are published in collective agreements, and we know exactly how much the average working person makes. But we do not know, and this bill will not tell us, how much executives are making.
What is the nature of the system of compensation in our society? How great in fact are the inequalities? If we are to have any degree of equality in our society, if we are to have decisions with respect to redistribution of wealth, decisions with respect to policies which will help Canadians in need of help, we simply have to have information with respect to the distribution of wealth and opportunity in our society.
This is why I find it strange that the government would take so long to bring in a bill on corporations and labour unions and do nothing to deal with a major gap in our legislation. This gap has been raised annually by hon. members of my caucus with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet). Most notably it was brought forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). For years he has been campaigning for the need to provide Canadians with information which is theirs by right. It is important to know just how serious the inequalities of wealth in our society have become and just how great is the gap between the rich and the poor.
Canada has the lowest rate of taxation on wealth of any country in the OECD. Canada also has the lowest rate of taxation on inheritances and on capital gains of any OECD country. These rates are lower than the ones of the Americans who are frequently cited by my friends on the right as being the wave of the future.
I find this animal called Liberalism strange. In its Ontario manifestation over the past weekend, it talked about the problems of distribution of wealth and opportunity in Canada and in Ontario. It talked about the need to bring in new legislation respecting capital gains, when it is the Liberal beast on that side of the House that is responsible for the taxation system which create this inequality. That Liberal beast created the loophole in capital gains taxation which allowed some people to benefit from inflation while others are hurt by it. It would be horrendous if it were not so funny.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said in British Columbia on Thursday that the Liberals were considering major changes in the banking system. This is the message the Minister of Agriculture is trying to get across to the audiences he is addressing throughout Canada. The leader of the Liberal party in Ontario told people that the distribution of wealth in Canada is a disgraceful situation. We know where the bottom line is; we know what really happens. The government brought in the Bank Act which did nothing to reform the banking system. It resisted every step of the way every progressive amendment put before it. It only accepted a minuscule number of them because the government was forced; it wanted to get the bill through. This is the reality.
The hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) and myself were present in the committee during those summer months. We know how interested the Liberal party is in reforming the banking system. Perhaps the Minister of Agriculture would do well to study the minutes of the committee meeting to know what the real Liberal party thinks.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on Bill S-10. The bill has been nicknamed "CALURA", or as my hon. colleague behind the curtain just said, perhaps it should be nicknamed "cholera". It sounds like the name of a perfume, but it does not smell like perfume when I read the bill.
I should like to deal with a few items in the bill so that the House will know exactly with what we agree and disagree. The object of the bill is to provide for the reporting of financial and other information of corporations and labour unions. That, in itself, is a worthy objective-the Government of Canada should know certain information about corporations and labour unions. The information should be available to the government for its own purposes. It will not be used for financial purposes because people report such information in their financial returns. When companies and labour unions are filing returns, there should be some guarantee that this information will not become the topic of conversation in coffee shops or beer parlours.
It is quite proper for information to be gathered, but another item in the bill which bothers me somewhat is the transferring of technological information from Canadians to foreign interests and from foreign interests to Canadians. I have searched the act and the bill in vain to find a definition of "technological transfers". It may be a very innocent item or it may be a very important item hidden by the fact that it is not very conspicuous in the bill.
A few years ago the House heard the metric system being discussed. In that bill there was a hidden section indicating the the standard or imperial system would be done away with; it was not emphasized. It should have been the major part of the bill because it concerned Canadians. I am wondering whether technological transfers is something similar. The minister mentioned that it was in the bill and that was all. As far as I can recall, he made no other comment with regard to technological transfers.
Technology is how we do things. For example, one company from the United States came to the country and spent millions of dollars developing a process for separating sand from the oil in the Fort McMurray area. The process belonged to that company; it was not required to give it to anyone else. It spent millions of dollars of its money to develop it. When Syncrude came on the scene, the great Canadian oil sands shared the information and received compensation for that sharing. In other words, it gave up part of its land it had secured through the proper process to Syncrude. It is a very important item. If technological transfers mean that these processes must be brought into the hands of the government through this board, and then they will be made available to others-and there may be leaks-it is very, very important to know exactly to what we are agreeing in regard to the bill.
Technological research is the basis of advancement. We must have research. When research is developed by an individual or a company and they apply under the laws of the
Corporations and Labour Unions
country for protection, they should have that protection. It should not be passed on to a government body. This is the part that worries me.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the findings in science and research, or whatever field, must have some protection, otherwise the initiative which brought it about in the first place is destroyed. Here there are these technological transfers without any definition, without saying what it is supposed to do or who is supposed to do it. Again, this is something about which I certainly disagree. If technological transfers were defined in the act, then we would know exactly what is involved. But it is not defined. This government is getting into the habit of doing just that. It included aboriginal rights in the Constitution and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) said today that it is not known what the term means so it must go before the courts for definition. He was deploring the fact that the courts decided against the Indian people before, yet he is saying that the courts much decide again. When will this government learn that when legislation is written that is the time to define the terms? That is an elementary principle in the writing of laws.
In 1978 the CALURA report which was tabled in this House reported that the top 500 non-financial enterprises accounted for 53 per cent of sales in Canada, 66 per cent of the profits and 70 per cent of the equity. Of that 500 some 274 were foreign-controlled corporations. In other words, without those foreign-controlled corporations the gross national product in this country would have been a great deal lower than it was.
Canada was made up of people who came from all countries of the world. Money, unions and corporations coming from the nations of the world combined together to make up Canada. They all came under Canadian law. We set the conditions. Alberta was a "have-not" province in the hungry thirties when some 52 per cent of our taxes went to the financiers to pay

June 22, 1981
Corporations and Labour Unions interest charges alone. What was the principle then? The money was going out. There was no control over that situation.
Then we wanted to get some money in order to develop. We went to eastern Canada, to the Bank of Canada, to Canadians, to England and to Germany. No one was prepared to invest their money in the province of Alberta. We then went to the United States. The Americans were prepared to invest their money in Alberta. They developed our oil and gas industry. That was the beginning of what we have today. Had that course not been followed we still might be a "have-not" province-the way this government likes to keep our provinces.
If the money had not come in the oil would not have been developed. We invited the Americans to come. They did so and worked under the conditions set out by the government of Alberta. They did not try to establish the rules; they obeyed them and became good corporate citizens.
This is an area in which the government shows day by day that it is lacking. It talks about Canadianization when it means nationalization. Which means that if you have a good thing you are liable to lose it in a short time because the government may take it over. Why does this government not have people come in, work under the rules of Canada and develop our gross national product? That is the way to develop the country. That is the way in which this country was developed, but now the government asks for all kinds of reports and information. Its own report, tabled in this House in 1978, indicates that over one half the sales, the profits and equity in non-financial enterprises would not have occurred had it not been for foreign-controlled companies working in this land under the rules and conditions which we set out.
What use will be made of the information for which we are asking? I think this is a very important item. Right now only the aggregates are available to other departments. They are then made public, as set out in the bill.
Bill S-10 re-establishes the conditions which existed before 1965 when the federal government had access to the financial information provided by individual companies. That provision was done away with in 1965. The government of the day wanted to give some credibility to the companies. It wanted the companies, the corporations and the trade unions to believe in it so it made the aggregates available to other ministries. But it did not make the financial statements of individual companies available.
That is not good enough for the government in power today. It wants to go back 16 years to 1965 in order to make the whole financial statement available to other departments. The bill sets out who will receive this information. It says that an official who is an officer, or another person taking his place, shall, where authorized by the Chief Statistician of Canada, on the request of any minister of the government, for any purpose relating to the determination of policy, make this information available.
The bill provides that, upon receipt of an application for inspection, payment of a fee not exceeding one dollar is required. I suppose that if the information is to be made
available it should be available to everyone. I do not think any individual wants to have his financial statement published in the press or made available for inspection to people off the street where it can become the talk at the coffee counters and the beer parlours of the nation. In the case of trade unions, all the information must be made available free of charge.
Who will be required to make these reports available, to provide this information? This is a good point in the bill. If the bill has any good points at all, this is fit. A corporation with assets exceeding $250,000 and/or sales amounting to more than $500,000 must file. That is the situation now. If enacted the bill before us will raise that amount to $5 million. It provides that any corporation with assets exceeding $5 million or sales amounting to more than $10 million must now file. Companies which had to file under the old legislation will not any longer have to go to the expense of filing, while the larger corporations and the labour unions will have to do so. According to the minister, there will be some 70,000 businesses affected which will have some redress from filling in all of these forms.
When we come to the labour unions part of the bill, the minister says Bill S-10 will lead to significant improvements in the administration of the act. I have searched to find out whether these significant improvements are for the unions of our country. I cannot find them in the bill. Perhaps the hon. minister will outline them when he is closing the debate. However, the one thing I did find is that the definition of "union" has been extended, and not restricted, to any association which regulates relations between employers and employees. Under the old bill, there are some stipulations under which a union did not have to comply. Now any and every union will have to supply the information. The international unions will have to report all direct revenues from Canadian subsidiaries, and also financial data of pension and strike funds, and report on their membership on a calendar year basis. I do not suppose there is anything particularly wrong with reporting on their membership.
I do not object to labour unions being required to give information on membership and other important matters to the government providing those items are then kept somewhat confidential. However, it seems to me that international unions are being pinpointed for special abuse. International unions have done a real service in this country. Anyone who knows the situation knows that the international unions have done a great deal. As a matter of fact, there have been times in this country where, had it not been for international unions, many of our workers would have gone hungry. I refer to the United Mine Workers of America.
I was raised in a coal mining area and I know what goes on in a coal mining area. There were times when we had no work, when Ontario was buying its coal from the United States and Canadian mines were idle, pretty much the way it is right now. We still buy large amounts of coal from the U.S.A. Not all mines stand idle, but all miners do not get the work. In
June 22, 1981

addition to that, we have coal in Alberta, in Canada, which has low sulphur content. But does one think we could use that to reduce acid rain? No. We keep on buying coal with much higher sulphur content from the U.S.A. to aggravate the acid rain problem.
However, the point I am making is that there were times when workers, through no fault of their own as there was no work available, would have gone pretty hungry had money not come from the international unions, from their American offices, to assist coal miners in this country. That is not a fairy story, that is the truth. The international unions have also shown a great deal of responsibility. I do not know of any union in this country which has been more responsible to the United Mine Workers of America. Did one ever hear of a union saying to the mine operator: "We are going to forgo even the cost of living increase in our wages this year because we know you are having a tough time keeping this mine open; we will forgo any increase just to keep our jobs? That happened in a mine in this country. The union showed responsibility as an international trade union. I think we should recognize that there is a place for unions and that we believe in the autonomy of unions. If the miners of this country want to work under the auspices of the United Mine Workers of America, why should we tell them that they cannot do that?
I remember one of the worst strikes I have ever seen, and I have gone through many of them. A union called the Canadian Union, which was simply the mouthpiece for the communist organization, tried to oust the United Mines Workers of America from authority in the coal mines in Canada. The coal miners caught on to the idea. They are autonomous. They have complete rule of their unions in this country. They do not take orders from another country. They objected to a communist inspired union, as its final and ultimate objective is to do away with unions altogether, under a communist regime. The Canadian Union lost out because the United Mine Workers held together. I remember the difficulties, trials and tribulations during that strike, when women with axes, brooms and shovels and men with clubs stood along the road to try to stop people from going to work in a strike which was called by this communist union known as the Canadian Union. The United Mine Workers were loyal to their own union and loyal to their own country and they refused to stop at that time. Therefore, do not tell me that international unions are all bad. Maybe some are bad, but a lot of them are good. I think we should give them credit where they deserve credit.
Again, in this country we have always had some freedom of choice. Why should our workers not decide what union they want and whether they want a Canadian union or an international union? There are disadvantages to both. However, our workers are not illiterate any more. They should have the choice. We should not be pinpointing an international union, requiring it to do things that we do not require of our other unions.
The international unions will have to report all direct revenues from Canadian subsidiaries and financial data pertaining to their pension funds. If other corporations have to report
Corporations and Labour Unions their pension funds, then I think international unions should also.
I would like to comment about strike funds. What concern is it of the government how much money workers put into a strike fund? I want to know why the government wants to know that kind of information. It is like a census form wanting to know how many toilets there are in a house. It is ridiculous information. No wonder our people are riled up about that long census form.
While I am on that subject, I am wondering what authority there is for the government to ask some people to fill in a short form while others must fill in a long form. Again, this is discrimination of some kind. Why do we not all have the same form if the government must have that information? What good is the information coming from one tenth of the population? What does that prove? We might as well let Gallup poll do it. It would not cause the taxpayer all the agony which is being caused through this census information. I believe in the census, but why is there a difference between Canadians, where some have to work hours on it and others can fill in the form in five minutes?

This strike fund is something I want to know about. What business is it of this government how much they have in their strike fund? It is not the government's money, it is the unions' money. It is none of the government's business. I know why the government wants to know. If there happens to be a strike, the government wants to know how long they can stay on strike, and maybe it leaks the information. No one believes in this government any more. It has no credibility. People will not trust it as far as they can see it or throw it. The government is concerned about a strike fund, but it is none of the government's business. This is the workers' own money. It is not the employer's business either. It is coming out of the pockets of the workers, and it is their business only.
The government has no right to this information by asking them to report how much money they have in a strike fund. That is ridiculous. It is their money. That can be resolved in the union meetings. It is none of my business and it is none of the government's business. I object to this type of thing being carried on in the name of government. It is just another one of these things, like the technological information, where the government tries to get information to which it is not really entitled and which it may well misuse.
Another section of this bill which is of concern is the penalties provision. We put the penalties in to try to force people to do exactly what we want them to do. The penalty under section 12(1) of the act is that the guilty party is liable,

June 22, 1981
Corporations and Labour Unions
on summary conviction, to a fine of $50 per day if the form is not filed. The bill provides for up to $250 per day. A very large corporation with bookkeepers, researchers and accountants would have no problem finding the information that is required but many of the smaller unions that rely on volunteer workers would not have the time to do this. The people there work after hours or give up their Sundays to do this type of thing. A $250 per day fine for failing to file a return would be difficult for them. The government has no business asking for all this information anyway and I do not think it is right. The fine is exorbitant and ridiculous for small unions. Because it has the law on its side, the government is trying to threaten people into doing something it knows they should not have to do.
We pass many of these laws in the way we passed some the other day. I have never seen anything so ridiculous as going through scores of pages without a chance to debate the legislation. We wonder why people do not want to obey the laws and we make it an offence if they do not, yet we do not have enough time to discuss them. They have not been carefully thought out, yet the government brings in closure to stop the House debating the bill properly.
This penalty is too high for many small unions, Mr. Speaker, and I want to go on record as saying that it should be reduced. The fine should vary in accordance with the offence. All offences are not the same and there should be no difficulty in setting out a range of fines instead of simply saying not exceeding so much. If the offence is committed in one province there may be a $10 fine, while in another part of that province or in a different province the fine could be $250. The government has given discretion to the courts but has not given them any guidelines.
Clause 8 of the bill provides to whom the information may be made available. A few moments ago I dealt with the matter of the unions providing the information free of charge.
In my view, this bill simply brings the government more into the lives of the people. Just the other day the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications (Mr. Stollery) praised the government for wanting more and more intervention and more and more regulation and defamed anyone who wanted deregulation.
Another thing that bothers me, Mr. Speaker, is that this bill will not create one job outside government. It will make things more difficult. Perhaps I should not say it will not create one job, as some large corporations may have to hire a full-time man to put together all this information that the government wants, to report the technological advances and so on. It will not create any work for labourers, however. Those people whose unemployment insurance is running out today cannot hope for a job as the result of this bill. The government could have brought in all kinds of bills that would create jobs in the country.

Why should they spend their time trying to create jobs in this country instead of thinking up ways of getting more information, more forms more regulation, more government and less gross national product?
The government talks about high interest rates stopping inflation and producing a higher gross national product. Why is that not happening? I do not see any increase in the gross national product. The government should encourage people to invest their money instead of making it almost impossible to do so. It should discourage the flight of capital into the United States. It should find a means to keep our rigs and money in this country instead of sending them to the United States to find oil for that country. If we kept them we would keep enough jobs as well; but this bill does not bring about any jobs. It is complete bureaucracy.
Small business in this country will receive some little benefit from this bill. If we take the minister's word, 70,000 of them will not have to fill out forms in the future. Many of them will still go under, however, because they cannot pay the high interest rates.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has said that the small business development bond will be helpful. It might if it were made available to everyone, but so many stipulations are attached that it is valuable to only a handful of people. A company has to be incorporated before it can receive benefit from that legislation. But thousands of farms and businesses in this country are not incorporated, Mr. Speaker, so they cannot make use of the lower interest rate of the small business development bond.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) made reference to the Farm Credit Corporation. That is a good organization and is useful to those who qualify for loans. But thousands of people do not. Sometimes it runs out of money before it can even start to deal with the line of applicants who want to develop their farms.
Small business is looking in vain for some help from this government but all it is getting is a regimented society. The inequalities and the gap are becoming greater and greater all the time. That situation was outlined a few moments ago by

the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) so I will not go over it again.
Instead of being anxious to get hold of Alberta's wealth, I wish the government would show a little interest in helping the other provinces to develop their resources and get things going in those provinces. That is what we need in this country. Thousands of other people would do the same thing if they were in this House today. They are sick and tired of regimentation, sick and tired of the government wanting to distribute wealth all the time.
Why does the government not help the provinces to create wealth? Each province in this country has a lot of potential. Would anyone invest their money under this government? No. It talks about Canadianization and nationalization and about how much it can get hold of, how much it can take. It takes and takes and takes, as it is doing from gasoline prices today. People are now waking up to the fact that the government has already gone way beyond the 18 cents per gallon that it denounced so wildly in the PC budget. It denounced that and now it is collecting far more.
The government talked about the "Tale of Two Cities" when it wanted to take one pound of flesh. It will take the pound of flesh and the blood and the bones and the grit as well. It wants the whole works and that is what is destroying this country today.
If the provinces were encouraged to develop their natural resources and if the people were encouraged to keep their money in the country instead of investing it in other countries such as the United States, and if our rigs were encouraged to stay here, things would be better. But the government will not even enter into an agreement with Alberta for oil at $20 per barrel. It is quite prepared to pay foreign countries $40 and $45 a barrel. But that would interfere with the government's plans for disunity in this country. The government would find out that small business would develop by the hundreds in this country if the incentive was there. We should have a bill to help develop our resources and do away with some of the inequalities.
The CALURA bill is going to make more book work for our unions and companies. It will not create any jobs in the country. The CALURA bill is not that important. I would rather have had a bill which would create wealth instead of bills that snatch on to some of the wealth after it has been created. We need a bigger gross national product, not a smaller one. That will not be done by regimentation but by encouraging people to invest their money in this country. That will be done by encouraging our people to use their creative abilities, our technological advances and our research. If we can do that, we can get this country moving again. But people look in vain for anything like that from this government.
Encouraging people to invest and use their creative abilities will build stronger provinces and a greater nation. But this government wants a central government which is going to control everything. This government does not care two hoots

what it does in trying to reach that objective. It will destroy the provinces. It will separate the country if necessary.
That is the sad story of what is happening in Canada today. It is a sad story about a government which does not care, that does not listen but is determined to build a centralist organization. The longer this government can keep each province in poverty, the better it likes it because then the government can say, "We will give it to you." Then when you get your bread from the government, you do what the government tells you to do.

Mr. Speaker, one of the great fears that we as members of Parliament have in opposition is the method of intrusion that this government is embarking upon into the Canadian way of life. This is not only in intellectual property or corporate property, but into the very privacy of our lives. Every aspect of our way of living is now being scrutinized by some government official. This has never happened before in Canadian history, but it is certainly very obvious that the government is now making a very major intrusion into the sanctity of the Canadian way of life.
For instance, the Constitution is a perfect example of what the government is up to. Bill C-57, which is to be voted on this evening, is the last chance, our last swing, that we will ever get as to what the government is doing in that legislation. It is very obvious what the government is up to. It is trying to get total control of our Canadian way of life.
It started some years ago in our armed forces. We saw centralized control. The three commanding heads of three departments were taken away and put under one head. Therefore, it is much easier for a centralized government to control the armed forces. This is happening all the way through our system. There are suggestions in this bill. I will read a portion of it to show what the government is doing. On page 11, Clause 2, we find the following sub-paragraph:
"(viii) the name and address of each employer resident in Canada with which the union or a local union or branch of the union has a collective agreement, and the number of male members and the number of female members of any local union or branch of the union covered by the collective agreement-
What difference does it make whether a member of the union is male or female? Surely they are entitled to be classed as a Canadian citizen and they are entitled to the right to membership in a union if they so desire. Why should the government want to know that? It means the records are always changing. As my colleague from Drumheller said, in some corporations there will have to be an extra person charged with the responsibility of keeping all the data up to date and filling in the questionnaires. All the costs associated with that will have to be added to whatever business it is. If it happens to be a labour union, the dues will have to go up. If it is a corporation or whatever, the cost will be passed on to the consumer. In summary, this is an added cost to our over-all system.
We have a government which has promised to do away with some of the paper burden. It is not doing away with it fast enough. There is a suggestion that raising the amounts to $150,000 and $5 million will eliminate some people. Yes, it

June 22, 1981
Corporations and Labour Unions
will. But with inflation as it is, for how long will they be eliminated? This is the question we have to ask ourselves when we are dealing with this type of legislation.
I think it would be much better if the government were to set some guidelines in the area of where it is going to cut back on the demand on the backs of Canadians. The load becomes too heavy. We have to recognize that this is a non-productive part of our business and our economy. What is happening to a greater degree in Canada is that too many are riding on the backs of business and there is not enough productive capacity. There has been too much of this tax taking and extra work in paper burden. If the government would change its policy to a greater degree, and much more quickly than it has up to the present time, then we would see Canadian business move ahead more quickly.
We have a $17 billion deficit in manufactured products in Canada. We have over one million unemployed. We have a tremendous amount of potential and we have a tremendous amount of natural resources. All we have to do is put those three together and we will start to resolve some of our major problems. This is the direction in which the government should be going. It should not be putting the extra load on to corporations that are struggling as a result of having to comply with government policy. This is one of the reasons we see so many of our corporations moving out of Canada, either going to the United States or, in some cases, to South America.
If many of these people involved in the corporations were assured that the information being given was relevant and would be used properly, that information would be given much more graciously than it is being given at the present time. We have to be careful. I must warn this House that, in my opinion, we have to be very careful when we allow governments to collect information, in view of what can be recorded now by various methods. Various people are able to have access to a computer system of knowledge. Who knows what will happen as a result of bringing all this information together? It has not been proven to us in the opposition nor to Canadians generally that there is a requirement for the massive interventionist attitude upon which this government has embarked. It is not only destructive to our Canadian way of life but it creates a fear. There is a lack of confidence on the part of many Canadians as to what the government is doing by collecting this information. I do not like what is happening.
As I said earlier, tonight we are passing Bill C-57. That bill makes a major intrusion into our Canadian way of life in a manner never witnessed before in Canada. One of the best examples is the newspaper industry. For the first time ever, civil servants with their rulers will be making assessments in the newspaper industry. For the first time ever we are going to have government inside the press rooms of our country.
I must impress upon hon. members the danger that creates for our Canadian way of life. Freedom of the press is one of the basic freedoms of this country. However, we are now going to have a bureaucracy moving into our press rooms. That is
very wrong. No doubt this data will all be collected so that when the time comes, and we hope this will never happen, a centralist government will have when it wants this centralized power. We have seen in our lifetime the dangers of centralizing power, knowledge and important information. I am convinced the Canadian people are travelling in the wrong direction under the administration of the present government and the centralist way they are being led.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the privilege of bringing this to the attention of the House. It is something I hope members opposite will give consideration to because their freedom is as much at stake as mine.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few comments on this very important bill. It is not receiving the attention in the media that it should. Perhaps many of them do not understand the seriousness and the complications of the legislation, which was pointed out by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers).
Our lead speaker, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), gave an example of what is happening under this government's regulations. I quote from his speech of June 17:
In the Thirtieth Parliament when I was doing work on a street view of corporate concentration, what attracted me to CALURA was four or five small businesses in Quebec which had been taken to court and fined under the powers of CALURA. Some of those businesses no longer exist. In fact, I do not know if any of them do. Those little businesses had to pay fines of $700 or $800.
Here is the startling point in the hon. member's remarks:
On the other hand, while doing my work on corporate concentration, I found that the holding company for Power Corporation had never filed under CALURA. If Power Corporation or the holding company had been treated in the same manner as these small businesses, which the government likes to talk to about protecting and reducing the burden on so much, the holding company for Power Corporation would have been subject to fines of over $3 million. However, they were not taken to court.
CALURA has been on my mind for some time. It is an important piece of legislation that has not been attended to for some time and that needs amending.
For many years it has been Liberal policy to be on the backs of small business. That is a classic example. It takes from the little guy and gives to the huge Power Corporation of Quebec.
We agree with the reporting part of the bill as well as that of union reporting, but not with the information aspect which demands that an inventory of technological information, intellectual property, trade marks and patents and so on be reported. It is highly interventionist.
This is an omnibus bill just as so many others have been. One example is Bill C-57, which automatically increases taxes for the handicapped, the beer drinkers and other groups across Canada. The element with regard to fines is overpowering for small business. There are excessive fines of $250 per day for not providing information. Under the metric law to be forced on the Canadian people, there will be heavy fines and jail sentences for those who do not comply.
Because the Liberals had to have their Constitution passed, Parliament is being forced to rush through important legislation such as this without giving it proper attention. It is not so much the bill we are opposed to but rather the way the Grits
June 22, 1981

will use the information. This bill will curtail individual rights and freedoms by unduly restricting and overextending the requirement of the reporting responsibility of small business.
I will give a few examples of over-regulation. The National Energy Program is having an absolutely devastating effect on the nation's economy, especially in my province of Manitoba where it practically closed down the whole oil exploration industry just as it was getting going. There could have been a real economic boom in Manitoba but this ridiculous NEP over-regulates the oil industry in the province of Manitoba and other provinces and is bringing the industry to a grinding halt. It only helps the economy in OPEC countries such as Venezuela and Mexico.
This is an interventionist policy of ill repute which threatens the theory of free enterprise. It is completely non-voluntary and requires an overly large amount of information. There is some connection between this bill, the strengthening of FIRA, the Competition Act and some provisions of the Constitution which impede the natural rights of Canadians. This type of legislation will make the empire builders within the Liberal government happy. It will give them a lot of work to do.
To give another example of what the National Energy Program will do and what it will cost the Canadian people, I want to quote from the June 6 edition of the Edmonton Journal:
It should be clear that Canadians are paying $43 a barrel for oil we had offered to sell last year for $20 a barrel.
That is a quote from the Alberta energy minister, Mr. Leitch. We can see what all this regulation is doing. It is a fantastic cost to the Canadian people. This overregulation interferes with the free enterprise system across the country. The literature being distributed in the ridings across the country of Liberal members of Parliament gives a completely false interpretation of the National Energy Program and the serious effects of the regulations contained in it. This literature talks about security as follows:
Canadians will again control their energy future through security of supply and independence from the world oil market.
That is a false statement. We are importing more and more oil. It is costing Canadian taxpayers $500,000 an hour to import foreign oil. Under the regulations made under the National Energy Program, by 1990 it will cost Canadians an additional $182 billion a year to import oil at heaven only knows what price per barrel.
The Liberal propaganda says the following about opportunity under the new energy regulation program:
Canadians will now have real opportunity to participate in the energy industry and to share in the benefits of industry expansion.
That is absolute rubbish. I have documentation here which shows that over 100 businesses in Alberta-and this is a statistic just for one individual area of Alberta-will be experiencing layoffs and cutbacks because of the new regulations contained in the National Energy Program. Where is the opportunity for them? This energy program provides a great
Corporations and Labour Unions
opportunity for the United States, and that is where most of the industry is going. Under "fairness" the propaganda says, and I quote:
Canadians will have a petroleum pricing and revenue-sharing regime that will be fair to all Canadians regardless of where they live.
What is fair about Canadian taxpayers having to spend $43 for a barrel of oil brought in from Mexico or Venezuela or other OPEC countries when it could be bought here in Canada for $20 a barrel? That is highway robbery. This is the kind of documentation the Liberals are distributing around the country. It is completely false and misleading. Why are they not telling the people about the businesses they are chasing out of the country? Why are they not telling Canadians about the adverse effects their energy policy has on businesses in eastern Canada? Why do they not tell that to the people of Ontario and Quebec? They should not be bringing in these ridiculous regulations which do absolutely nothing about energy self-sufficiency in this country.
I would like to give another example of how Liberal regulation affects various businesses. The Chevron oil company in Vancouver volunteered the following information recently: Chevron Canada Limited has to complete 491 monthly, quarterly and annual reports for the federal government which are then inspected by 14 federal agencies, 19 provincial agencies and 8 municipal departments; this apparent duplication of government inspection and excessive paper work must be monitored more closely.
As far as we in the Conservative party are concerned, it should be reduced. We had taken steps to deal with this. Duplication and all this regulation was on the agenda for the first ministers' conference of December 15, 1979. The government of our leader, who was then the prime minister, was going to do away with this waste, duplication and overregulation. We were going to do something about it, but are the Liberals doing anything about it? No, they most certainly are not.
Just recently I learned from the Manitoba Teachers Society of another example. That society informs us that there are over 70 federal agencies involved in education and educational research. The Canadian Parks Association points out that there are over 66 federal government agencies duplicating services provided in the area of recreation. Why on earth do we need that many regulations and that many departments at the federal level involved in recreation and teaching? The bureaucracy has complete control of this Liberal government. This government has allowed the bureaucracy to continue its overregulation and empire building within the departments. If bureaucrats can come up with new regulations or new programs to set up new departments or Crown corporations, they have the full co-operation of the Liberal party.
It is predicted that the National Energy Program and the new regulations I mentioned earlier will cause the loss of 60,000 jobs by mid-summer. I did not see that in the Liberal propaganda being sent out to constituents. Liberal backbenchers should be telling their constituents what the ridiculous program they are forcing on Canadians is doing in relation to

June 22, 1981
Corporations and Labour Unions jobs being lost. I would like them to explain to me how the loss of 60,000 jobs will benefit us.
One of the regulations in Bill C-57 imposes another 9 per cent tax on prosthetic devices. These devices are used by the handicapped. Prostheses used on legs and ankles are excepted. This tax was soundly criticized in the House last week as a blatant slap in the face of the handicapped during the International Year of the Disabled. This government is imposing additional taxes through regulations which will be passed year after year. Taxes will be increased by order in council. This government will not have to come back to Parliament. There will be more regulation and more taxation without even having to come to this House. The government is going to tax artists who create original prints. This will affect members of Eskimo co-operatives in northern Canada whose prints are considered highly valuable works of art around the world.
Nobody escapes the clutches of this Liberal party. The newspaper industry has expressed grave concern about a 9 per cent tax on advertising supplements which, the industry says, threatens its livelihood. This government is threatening everyone, regulating everyone and taxing everyone.
They say a picture is worth a thousand words, and I would just like to refer to a cartoon which was in the Winnipeg Free Press last week. It showed three thugs in a jail cell along with a little Canadian citizen. He had just been put into the cell with them. The three thugs asked what he was in jail for. "Oh," he said, "I would not tell the government how many toilet seats I have". The question is, are the hurts worth the gains you get, can you properly concentrate or take it easy?
The council pointed out that what we need is more productivity and less regulation.
A report in the Toronto Star said this about this Economic Council report:
-while the Economic Council's provocative report sounds a timely note of caution on the subject of government regulatory involvement in the economy, it also underlines the importance of those regulations that ensure all Canadians a better quality of life. Reform should be on the agenda, but not hastily.
The ECC also point out in an article in the Montreal Gazette of June 15:
Overregulation of the Canadian economy costs several billion dollars a year. That is perhaps $120 per Canadian, perhaps more-say, $500 a year for a family of four. Most of that money comes straight out of our pockets, not governments'.
All it is is job-creation programs thought up by empire builders. I do not know why the Liberals are not commenting on this today. It would be nice to know how many Liberals in the House support these regulations, how they can justify
costing a Canadian family $500 a year. Do they actually support this type of program? If they do, let them get up and give us an explanation why. We do not see the need for them at all. We do not see a need for finding out how many bathrooms and toilet seats people have, Mr. Speaker.
The Winnipeg Free Press, in an editorial on June 11, has pointed out their feelings on the reforming of regulations, as follows:
-the Economic Council of Canada has offered some sensible recommendations aimed at creating compatibility in the marriage that exists between the Canadian economy and the regulations that affect it. The recommendations suggest moves that could make the marriage work to the better satisfaction of both parties, rather than advocating a quick and final divorce.
It urges the abandonment of regulations that have lived longer than the problems they were designed to correct, and the provision of flexibility in others to reflect the changing conditions of the marketplace.

I have referred to this before, Mr. Speaker, but I think it is worth mentioning again. Some citizens are so concerned about government regulations that they are putting full page ads in newspapers. There are a lot of people examining what this Liberal government is doing, and they are putting their money where their mouth is by paying for ads concerning these ridiculous programs and regulations.

Particularly small business has been fined under CALURA, not the bona fide large corporations such as the Power Corporation which was mentioned a few moments ago. As I said, we are sliding down the slippery road to a unitary state. We are becoming a controlled society. We are controlled more and more by the present government.
When we received the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the House in 1968, we also received 1984 early. Since he assumed office, the state has encroached more and more upon business and upon our citizens, as per this bill. "Big Brother" is constantly looking over our shoulders, with a survey here and a questionnaire there, just as this bill indicates. Consolidated financial statements will be obtained directly from enterprises through questionnaires-state interference. Approximately eight existing questionnaires will be integrated into one, supposedly to reduce the paper burden. The point is that they are questionnaires and they represent going into patents and other such items-straight intervention in our system.
We have heard much about the need to lessen the paper burden on business, but it is only lip service, as any businessman will tell us if he is questioned. It is only government public relations in action. There is a lot of it going on now and government has become the biggest advertiser in Canada. The fact is that the paper burden is not being lessened, it is being increased.
The private sector of the country keeps the country in spending money. It generates the wealth which unfortunately the government dearly loves to redistribute. The government fails to realize-especially those members opposite who have never been in business-that it has been slowly strangling the goose which lays the golden egg with overregulation, big brotherliness, government interference, crippling taxation, direct and indirect, and the lack of an industrial strategy. Where is the industrial strategy about which we have heard so much? I have not seen it. Also it neglects research and development. We all know what a half of 1 per cent in research and development will do for the country. It will do a lot more than Bill S-10.
Through its ambitious social programs, more ambitious than those of our wealthy neighbours to the south, the government has chipped away and eroded the work ethic of the entire country. It is a sad thing to see in the youth. The government has made it more attractive financially to collect UIC than to work. Now we are faced with Bill S-10. It has placed a staggering debt load on the backs of Canadians. Our taxes are high enough but our real tax toll is the combination of
corporate and personal income taxes, the accumulated debt, and the oil and service charges which must go to discharge the tremendous borrowings of this great Big Brother.
I do not believe anyone in the government actually calls out for the business community. No one in the government understands what it is like to attempt to make it in the cold, corporate world of big or small business. Canadian business needs a hand up, not handouts. It does not need Bill S-10 to overregulate it. Canadian business needs the government off its back. Canadians need an end to the Big Brother phenomenon.
I have a speech which was made by the former president of the treasury board. It is entitled "How we became a socialist state". It pointed out the encroachment of government, through legislation such as Bill S-10, to compile information which is not needed to run the country, for it to be rich, powerful and strong again. It is encroachment of government; it is intrusion of government. It is the imposition of government will against that of the business community. Bill S-10 is just another law restricting our rights. We do need acts restricting corporations and the creation of wealth. We need greater production, not another paper burden.
Every move of the government is toward centralization. This was pointed out time and again under Bill C-48, another form of overregulation. As a small businessman I am confronted with capital expenditures. It is bad enough to cope with a 20 per cent interest rate, let alone cope with the bureaucracy of increasing paper burden and less rights.
This bill is more interference in the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act. It is government poking its nose into the business of private corporations. It is regressive, not progressive, legislation. I presume Bill S-10 is the preamble to the introduction of the Competition Act, and Lord knows what we will find in it.
The information aspect of CALURA frightens me. Will the financial statements of corporations be made public? Who will get their hands on this information? Multimillion dollar corporations file, others do not. It makes one ask why. Who can have the information in this bill? Obviously the government, but who else under section 8? I do not know.
The current definition of "labour unions" liable to report under the act is being improved to cover all labour unions with one hundred members or more resident in Canada. Supposedly, this was to ensure the widest possible coverage and, hence, completeness of data on labour unions. This is nothing but more government interference.
Why does the government need such information? International unions will report all direct receipts from their Canadian affiliates and all expenditures directly attributable to their operations in Canada. Is this not denigrating some of the great labour unions? Also, all unions will report information separately on each of their special funds, such as pension and strike funds. Why is this necessary? It is just more government interference. This provision was supposedly to broaden the
June 22, 1981

reporting of financial data. I guess it will. It will permit a better presentation of union finances. It will interfere with every union in this country. The government will be in their hip pockets and looking over their shoulders every waking minute. Membership data of individual unions will be made available to federal and provincial government departments for analysis and publication purposes, thereby reducing possible duplication of reporting by union locals. Where are the magnificent benefits to the unions in this bill? I fail to find any in what I have just stated.
From looking at this bill it appears to me as though international unions are coming under special reporting conditions. Even their strike funds will be affected. I do not think we want that situation in Canada. The government says that 70,000 small businesses will not have to report, that the paper work will mysteriously disappear. I think everyone on this side of the House knows for sure that will never happen. The provisions have been changed from reporting $250,000 in assets and $500,000 in sales to $5 million in assets and $10 million in sales. In my view, that is not an improvement. It smacks of crass socialism, of government riding shotgun on technological transfers. It all adds up to one thing-government intervention, stateism, centralization, nationalization, whatever you want to call it.
Bill C-48 was mentioned by my colleague from Winnipeg. He said the provisions therein were not for Canadianization but purely and simply for nationalization. Bill C-48 smacks of government interference, just as Bill S-10 does. This is overregulation, which is driving our Canadian dollar crazy and causing our interest rates to climb. I am wondering what this House is all about if it is not to debate bills to tremendous importance such as Bill S-10. In my view, Canadians are over-regulated and we will be more so once Bill S-10 is enacted.
It has been estimated that every man, woman and child in Canada could be regulated by government up to a value of $500. It is estimated that the cost of importing foreign oil to every man, woman and child in Canada is $150. Recently a representative of General Motors came to speak to our caucus. If people understood the costs of a General Motors car which are directly attributable to government regulation, they would be staggered. We have socialist, stateist policies. Our country was not built by overregulation or by government interference in our unions.
If we took the earth's surface and reduced it to one little country of a square mile and one tenth, with a population of 1,100 we would find that of those 1,100 some 22 would be communists, 440 would be under the direct control of communism, and 814 would be ignorant, poor or hungry. Only 286 would have sufficient food, clothing and shelter. Of the 1100 some 66 would be North Americans. Those 66 North Americans would own just 6.6 per cent of the land and 58 per cent of the wealth. They would produce 37 per cent of the food and electrical power, 50 per cent of the copper, iron and steel and 34 per cent of the coal. They would own 66 per cent of the automobiles, telephones, radios and televisions.

That will not be allowed to carry on if we have much more overregulation of our industries through measures such as Bill S-10. Those 66 North Americans would have 11 times more orchestras, groups, schools, museums, books and laboratories. That has been our legacy as a free enterprise system. The 66 North Americans would have 17 times more personal possessions than the other 1,034. A full 99 per cent of them would own a refrigerator, a telephone and a television. Some 80 per cent would own a washing machine and 92 per cent would own at least one car. Some 55 per cent of the goods in the world in the last 10,000 years have been produced in North America over the past 200 years.
Those are amazing facts, Mr. Speaker. Is this the result of socialism, state control and such measures as Bill S-10? No, Mr. Speaker. It has been accomplished by free enterprise, something the government across the way has forgotten. We must remember that as Canadians we are 10 per cent of the population figure I have just mentioned.
Why have Canadians been great? And we are great. It is because so far we have been free. We have not been overregulated. We have not had socialistic points of view forced on us in the past, as we are having them forced upon us now. We have been free to live and work under the free enterprise system.
Another word which I think members opposite have forgotten in their zeal for overregulation is the word "profit". It is a sad thing that too many people today have forgotten that word, including high school and college graduates, bureaucrats, members of Parliament including the entire New Democratic Party. Bill S-10 is designed to overregulate on the one hand and deregulate on the other. It does not assess what we really need, which is an increase in production. A great many people in this House, especially hon. members to my left, think that a capitalist is an elephant jumping up and down in a yard full of chickens screaming "Every man for himself'. To them, making a profit is a vice.
Winston Churchill is a great favourite of mine. One of the best quotes of his was not the one about fighting on the beaches or "Never in the field of human conflict has so much been owed by so many to so few", but "It is a socialist idea that making profits is a vice; the real vice is making losses". This government is making a loss by overregulation, by centralization and by taking us down the slippery road to socialism. The facts of life are that nothing happens until something is sold. By overregulating industry you do not sell things. You do not have a productive country. The socialistic policies in the handouts which this government makes are in some cases much needed, but we cannot afford to make them in this country because of the huge deficit we have incurred unless we increase productivity and meet the situation head on.
The facts of life are that profits make everything happen in our society. Without profits nothing happens. Our present government is not profiting. It must be made to take a look at the economic fiasco it is making of our free enterprise system. It is hitting at industries by giving more paper burden to corporations such as General Motors. Our gross national
