Mr. Speaker, I was involved in a debate last week which caused me at the time to raise the question of why the government should decide at that time to introduce the matter then before the House. This was either on Monday or Tuesday of last week. It was Monday, because that was their allotted day, so to speak, and they decided to talk about foreign affairs, and to go on from that to the North-South dialogue.
I asked a question right at the outset of my speech then. I asked why the government should have decided to introduce at that time for the second time in a decade, by a government motion, a matter for debate covering foreign affairs. I did not get a very satisfactory answer and I suspected that it had something to do with the delay in the ruling to be handed down by the Supreme Court of Canada.
I am forced to ask again why it is that today, June 22, a bill should be introduced to this House, presumably on the basis of the government's set of priorities, that was passed by the Senate on December 11, 1980. I am not complaining about some of the matters that intervened, but I would ask if the government has nothing more important than this to introduce as we approach the summer recess. It causes me to speculate a little bit about the intentions of the government in introducing a measure of this sort at this time and to regard its priorities as being weird and beyond the comprehension of an ordinary citizen such as I.
I should like to draw attention to another aspect of the preparation and presentation of this bill, Mr. Speaker. When I examined it to see if there was something I wanted to say about it, I took it for granted that it would deal with amendments to the Corporations and Labour Unions Act and, as with other bills, assistance would be provided on the right hand facing page regarding the existing legislation being amended. It may be that bills that come to us from the Senate do not contain such provisions. Nevertheless, I think it ought to be the

June 22, 1981
Corporations and Labour Unions
rule that when dealing with an amending bill there should be readily available to us, on the right hand page, as is normal with Commons bills, the provisions now on the statute book which the bill is intended to amend.
In order to see what this bill aims to do, I had to go back to the Revised Statutes, which are in themselves invaluable but a little bit cumbersome. The text of the act that is being amended appears in the Revised Statutes of Canada, Chapter 31. That chapter, with all its attachments, is 17 pages long while the amendments contained in this bill run to 15 pages. To a considerable extent there are deletions from the original act, but there are also some lengthy additions. All the complaints we have been listening to about reducing the need to report are an oversimplification of the amendments being suggested to the Revised Statutes of Canada, Chapter 31.
The paper burden notion has been before us on many occasions. It is within my recollection as a member of this House that a new committee was set up called the Joint Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. I am not a member of that committee. It deals with the amount of regulation of our society that is achieved by ministerial discretion or by statutory instruments which regulate. I shall come to the matter of ministerial discretion and the regulation which the minister may or is required to produce under the amendment before us. Members of that committee ought to be wondering, as I am, why we are adding to, rather than subtracting from, the number of regulations under which we suffer in this country.
The government put up one speaker on this bill. As well, there were complaints and specious points of order in the last half hour by a minister who suggested that the member then on his feet had not read the bill. I wonder whether the bill has been read by anyone at all on the other side.
Is anyone over there aware of any super-regulation being imposed by this bill? The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) mentioned one or two items in the bill and the returns that will have to be made as a result of them. They include the very matters already provided in the Income Tax Act by corporations and unions, and now another element comes into it.
We have just finished the 1981 census, Mr. Speaker. I am sure that every member of the House received complaints of one kind or another about the questions asked in the census. Some of the complaints were like this: "Only a month ago I filled in my income tax return. Why do you have to know the details again? How well are you going to preserve the confidentiality of the information?" The confidentiality assigned to statistics obtained and presumably analysed and incorporated into graphs by Statistics Canada is of great concern to many people. The secrecy element is another concern, and if someone had to fill out the long form, all the particulars of a family, which are none of his business, would be known to the census taker. One wonders whether it is really any business of Statistics Canada to require the information. If someone's income falls within the $10,000 to $20,000 bracket, that is fine; but particulars of gross income were required in some
census forms. Therefore, I think we are entitled to ask, and we would be remiss in our duties if we did not ask, the purpose for which all the information required to be produced by corporations and unions under Bill S-10 is going to be used.
I am looking square at a couple of officials who will probably be able to answer that question, but I doubt if there is anyone here in the House who would be able to answer it.
Have these additional bits of material been required of the Canadian people, corporate or trade union, in order to increase the bureaucratic power of some because he finds that he is not quite fully occupied with the material he has available to him, that he would like to get a little bit more? I think that is a possibility. Much of the information could be obtained by cross-checking in a confidential manner with the income tax department. It is within the walls of the Government of Canada. The information is provided in income tax returns. I see no reason why, if it is needed for any particular reason, it should not be transferrable on demand and under conditions of confidentiality from one department to another. But no, we want it all again. Take the small business person who runs a florist shop on the corner. The requirement to produce statistics to the government add overhead in an immeasurable way. I use "immeasurable" in the sense that it is beyond measure. There is no reason why that florist should either have to hire an accountant, on the one hand, or spend hours after closing time to fill out the forms that are demanded by Statistics Canada in order to fulfil their petty dreams or their petty requirements.
There is, as has been said on more than one occasion, an invasion of the privacy of the small enterprise, the corporation or the union in this particular bill. I do see a fairly large component of Parkinsonianism entering into the rationale behind these amendments. It is very difficult to check, of course. Still, I cannot understand why it is there.
With specific reference to the text of the bill before us, 1 notice Sections 3 to 6 of the original act, Chapter 31 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, are repealed. The replacements are given. Sections 3 to 6 occupy pages 2 to about page 7 in the original document, but the replacement occupy pages 3 to 10. So we have seven pages to replace three. And this is a simplification, we are old, of a bill so as to reduce the amount of reporting required. I question that, given the particulars required. Ones mentioned by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) are: the name of the corporation, the address of the head office and the manner in which the corporation was incorporated. Surely these particulars are on 80 files in this country, and yet Statistics Canada requires it again? For what purpose? Surely the name of the corporation would suffice?
In addition to that, the bill goes on to ask the manner in which the corporation was incorporated, the amount of the share capital, the number of issued shares and, in the case of corporations having 50 shareholders or less, the number of shares of that class held by persons having addresses shown in
June 22, 1981

the relevant records of the corporation, and so on. The very reading of these amendments, these shortenings of the original act, in themselves tax the imagination. Let us take the case of a florist, a wholesale flower distributor, or a nursery. Under this act these businesses would be required to produce this material once a year. I ask hon. members why. Why are they being burdened with this nonsense material?
There is another element here which concerns me. It goes back to a matter of ministerial discretion and regulation. On page 8 in clause 4.1(3) we find first:
The minister may, where he considers it advisable, authorize or require any holding corporation to file separate sets of financial statements in respect of itself and its subsidiaries-
Here we have the minister intervening for the first time with a discretionary power. I have already mentioned the problems we have had, and the need to set up a special committee about ministerial discretion. But in clause 4.2(2), again on page 9, we find:
-a return in the prescribed form specifying such information as the governor in council may prescribe relating to transactions involving transfers of technology-
What is this all about? Supposing that a transfer of technology is from Algoma Steel to Ipsco. Is that a concern of any government? This is a business transaction, a transaction between two corporate entities within Canada. Why should they be required to report that? What about a transfer of technology outside of Canada? I see, reading further, the following:
-to the holding corporation or any of its subsidiaries from persons not resident in Canada.
These are business transactions. What is Statistics Canada going to do about this? Is it going to report to the Foreign Investment Review Agency? Is that its policing function? Has it taken on this function? Therefore, we have a dual complaint: ministerial discretion, on the one hand, and the requirement to report transfers of technology, on the other.
Again we find in Section 4.2(2) the following:
-the governor in council may prescribe relating to transactions involving transfers of technology in the reporting period to the corporation from persons not resident in Canada.
Supposing Algoma Steel does get a process from Bethlehem Steel in the United States. Is it required under law to report it to the Government of Canada? I am at a loss to understand why it should. There is no reason at all. I hope some members on the other side will realize what is being asked of our various industries and trade unions. Their privacy is being invaded as never before.
We are now confronted with technological transfers. This bill used to be known as CALURA, which sounds like an Irish folk song, "Calura-lura-lie". With the introduction of the transfer of technology I suppose we will now have to call it CALUTTRA, the corporations and labour unions and technical transfers returns act. I cannot see any other name for it. It
Corporations and Labour Unions
destroys much of the harmony of that beautiful, lilting CALURA, but CALUTTRA I suppose it will have to be.
With regard to this technical transfer notion, I realize in one clause there is no requirement-"shall be deemed not to include any scientific or technical description of any product or process". Thank goodness for that. At least copyrights, trade marks and patents are safe.
That still does not explain why Statistics Canada has to know about these transfers, whether in or out of Canada, when they are covered by patents, copyrights or trade marks. However, they seem to feel they need to know. I see the members over there sitting back and not worrying one whit about it, which disturbs and distresses me. I will leave the comments on labour unions to some others.
Section 7(1) of the original act has been amended. There on summary conviction the fine did not exceed $50 for each day of such default. It is not surprising to learn that inflation has set in and instead of $50 it will now be $250 a day. The fine has been increased fivefold since the original passage of the act. Now any corporation that fails to file with the Chief Statistician of Canada its return for the reporting period every year or to comply with subsection 6(2), that is the one involving transfers of technology, will be liable to fines up to $250 per day so long as the default continues. I see by jumping over to page 13 that that same fine, instead of being probably $25 with respect to a union, has gone to $250 for each day of such default on summary conviction if the report has not been produced.
All things considered, I have my misgivings about the need for this bill. I would have been quite happy to see an amendment withdrawing Chapter 31 because it really does not produce much of value except perhaps for the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to know where he can levy his taxes. Maybe that is the reason. Maybe at the end of my speech I have discovered the rationale of the whole amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not often rise to participate in a debate on this subject. However, the minister having invited me to read the bill, I am unable to resist participating for a very few minutes.
Despite what the minister says, Bill S-10 is a confusing bill that is bound to add a fair amount of difficulty to conducting business in this country. I will try to stick as closely to the bill as I can. I will begin with the definitions and ask the House to note that the reporting period, which is spoken of quite a bit, is different for some businesses and some unions. The definition is a period that lasts not less than 12 months and not longer than 53 weeks after its commencement, and that ends between November 1 of one calendar year and January 31 of the following calendar year.
There are a few mysteries I hope will be cleared up when the minister speaks on this bill about the corporation, which is defined as a holding corporation.
A corporation is the holding corporation of another corporation if that other corporation is its subsidiary.

June 22, 1981
Corporations and Labour Unions
One should not be surprised that the next section puts it backwards:
A corporation is a subsidiary of another corporation if it is controlled by that other corporation.
That is fine except a little later on in the bill one finds:
-one corporation is affiliated with another corporation if one of them is the subsidiary of the other-
It rather confuses one as to how this could be true if a corporation is a subsidiary of another corporation that is controlled by that other corporation. They should really decide if it is a subsidiary or affiliate and preferably not have both at the same time.
When looking at page 8 of the bill, I became rather concerned about the role played nowadays by the Chief Statistician of StatsCan. My thought here was, "StatsCan, what are you doing?" StatsCan are apparently doing what the Department of National Revenue did heretofore. There was a time when business details were considered confidential to business-industrial confidential. One could ask the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) about details of the business conducted between McDonnell Douglas and the Canadian government. He would say he cannot tell you what the bids were on this, or what the bids were on that, or the offers on one plane or another, because it is industrial confidential.
The government insists in this bill that each business must produce, not for the Department of National Revenue but for Statistics Canada, the following:
(a)	a balance sheet showing the assets and liabilities...
(b)	a statement of investments of the corporation ...
(c)	a statement of income for the reporting period,
id) a statment of retained earnings...
(e) a statement of changes in financial position-
Why does StatsCan need this information? The Department of National Revenue would refuse you flatly if you asked for this information of any company or individual in Canada, yet we are going to entrust it to StatsCan which, as we all know, has the security of a leaky sieve. Businesses do not appreciate having anyone other than the Department of National Revenue ask for business details in this manner.
I am puzzled too about returns on transfers of technology which every holding corporation has to turn in. There is a definition of technology, but there are excuses by which corporations can be allowed out of that requirement. For instance, it says on page 9-perhaps I had better read it-the following:
Every holding corporation ... shall... file with the Chief Statistician of Canada not later than March 31 ... a return in prescribed form specifying such information as the governor in council may prescribe relating to transactions involving transfers of technology-
Two paragraphs later it says:
For the purposes of this section, information relating to transactions involving transfers of technology shall be deemed not to include any scientific or technical description of any product or process.
What on earth, then, is technology? It is baffling. In one place it says the transfer of technology, and in the next clause it excludes everything one always assumed was technology.
If you try to get out of sending in this return, there is a very uncharming, if I can use that word, or a very disagreeable clause, namely, Clause 6 on page 9, which says:
The Chief Statistician of Canada may, by notice in writing, request proof from any corporation that fails to file or fails to complete any part of a return required under this part that it is not subject to the application of this part in respect of the return or of the part of the return not completed.
In other words, you are absolutely guilty unless you can prove your innocence. I thought this assumption of guilt went out of vogue some one thousand years ago. I hope some way can be found by which the innocent-until-proved-guilty part of our common law can be retained, other than Clause 6 on page 9.
If you do not provide this notice, the notice is good only for ten days.
A corporation shall, within ten days after it receives a notice under subsection (1), furnish the Chief Statistician of Canada with the proof requested in the notice or file or complete, as the case may be, the return in respect of which the notice was given.
Ten days' notice to a business to produce the reasons it should not have to produce that file and proof of it is totally unrealistic. It is totally unrealistic to expect a firm of any size to do that within ten days.
I notice that labour unions do not have to comply if they have fewer than one hundred members resident in Canada. I suppose we can get this information at the committee stage, but I am curious as to how many unions in Canada have fewer than one hundred members resident in Canada and as to whether they might not prefer to break into branches of unions to ensure that they do not have to comply with some of the faulty law implicit in this bill.
At page 11 it says:
(a) a return in the prescribed form containing the prescribed information
including the following particulars:
This is not later than 90 days. However, this deals with unions. Let us go back to where businesses are dealt within the descriptions of the reporting stage. For unions the period is between November 1 of one calendar year and January 31 of the following calendar year, yet in the case of businesses this return has to be in by the end of March. If their reporting period ends January 31 and the return has to be in by the end of March, that is only two months which is allowed instead of 90 days. It seems that some of these corporations being spoken of could be very large indeed, and they would have to do in two months what a small union would have to do in three months. I think there should be a little more equity in that respect.
I am pleased to have participated in this debate. There are so many things wrong with the drafting of this bill and there has been so much confusion created one could almost take this as a textbook example of the burden placed on businesses and unions to comply with regulations. There is no apparent need for many of the regulations. I am particularly concerned that Statistics Canada should be requiring so many returns-which
June 22, 1981

are usually confidential-from firms which try to conduct business and keep this country going.

Mr. Speaker, in joining in this debate on Bill S-10 I suggest to many members in this House that if they feel that this bill is something of a routine nature or something the House might rubber stamp or pass without proper examination and debate, I feel they are overlooking some of the very serious implications inherent in the bill. It is a sleeper. In many ways this bill demonstrates the tremendous paper load the federal government places not only on businesses but also on labour unions in this country.
What I will try to point out in my remarks is that there is a serious question as to why we are passing this bill in its present form. I followed the minister's speech in the House, I read the Hansard report of his speech, and I was surprised to find that at no point did the minister attempt to justify the continuation of the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act. Instead, he tried to slide this bill through by saying it is going to be less onerous. Why should it be onerous at all to the Canadian businessman or to the Canadian labour union? I think a case can be made to show that this government should be taking steps we had intended to take when we were in power, namely, to trim government regulations regarding statistical information. The program we were putting into place was to relieve business of much of the paper work which governments and bureaucracies behind governments love to foster. There is a serious question as to why we should permit the government to bring in the bill in its present form.
I say that because I think we often overlook the true impact of what we are talking about here. Let us first ask ourselves whether this statistical data is relevant. If statistics are to mean much, they should be fresh, accurate and recent. And, of course, they must be relevant to what people are interested in.
On the first question-is the statistical information fresh- as we know, on December 15 last the minister tabled the last Corporation and Labour Unions Returns Act report. For what year? Was it for 1980 or 1979? No, it was for 1978, two years after the fact. In December of last year we were finally furnished with the report dealing with corporations as of two years earlier. At the same time two other reports were filed. One was on labour unions and was called "Catalogue 71-202 Annual". The other crafty little document was called "Catalogue 71-202S". It was a supplement dealing with labour unions which gave much more intimate details concerning the labour unions of this country.
I mention this because I suggest that any statistical compilation which is more than two years old before people who might be interested in the data have access to it cannot be represented as being fresh information which industry, labour unions and government anxiously await. I suggest instead that the type of material we have before us fits better into the general category of what is gathered in a census, which is what we went through on June 3; in other words, information catalogued from time to time but certainly not on a quarterly basis. There is probably no necessity to have it even on an annual basis.
Corporations and Labour Unions
When I take you through some of the detail, Mr. Speaker, on the cost to the Canadian consumer, the businessman, the worker, members of a labour union, I think there is a very serious question as to why we should continue the act at all. I say this because I note the minister, who has repeatedly interrupted some of our speakers, rose and said: "The bill was introduced in 1962 by the then Diefenbaker government." We do not deny that, but I would suggest that is reflective, if you like, of this rather stale, archaic type of government we have in power today. They suggest that because something was introduced by our government-and I would suggest to you that it was relevant in 1962-almost 20 years later it should be left on the statute books notwithstanding the tremendous differences there are on reporting by labour unions, corporations and individuals today a compared to 1962. That is the difference, and this sleepy old reactionary government is not up with the times. They do not seem to realize that in a modern day society it is government that is lagging, not business; it is government dragging business back because it just cannot keep up with them. Here you have an example where they suggest that something introduced about 19 years ago should be left on the statute books just because it was introduced 19 years ago.
Let me take you to my next point, Mr. Speaker, which is perhaps even more serious. It deals with the question of cost. What does it really cost the Canadian consumer? Let there be no mistake, people may say: "Well, what does it cost business, corporations or labour unions?" The ultimate person who pays when there is unnecessary cost is the consumer. Here is what the minister said in the House upon the conclusion of his introductory remarks on the bill. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that I asked him this:
Could the minister tell the House whether any evaluation was made during that study of what is the cost of complying under the act for business and for consumers throughout Canada? Is there some estimate as to what it is costing businessmen to comply with the act as it now exists, and can the minister give us any estimate as to what it will cost businessmen to comply with the new act if it is passed in its present form?
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, the minister replied:
I do not have with me any information in terms of the total cost to any individual company of completing a form on an annual basis. However, I would suggest to the hon. gentleman that it would not appear to be a concern of any of the companies with whom we have had exchanges.
In all fairness, Mr. Speaker, how can a minister come into this House and say it has never been of concern to any of the companies with which he has had exchanges when the selfsame government in, I believe, 1978, in a return given to a committee of this House pointed out there were 124 corporations with assets of over $5 million each that had not complied with the various forms under this act. That was in 1978, in relation to 1976 data. There were 12,000 corporations in total that had not supplied the information two years after the fact back in 1978. Yet we have a minister with the audacity to come in here and say the government has heard of no troubles as far as corporations are concerned.
I point this out because I think it is relevant that we review exactly what we are talking about here. Many of the speakers

June 22, 1981
Corporations and Labour Unions have referred to questionnaires and the fact this data is prepared therefrom. What is the nature of these questionnaires? Let us take a look first at the eight questionnaires business is now asked to fill in which have some relevance to this bill we now have before us, namely Bill S-10. If you like, I will challenge the minister on this. I will bet that the minister has not read those eight questionnaires. In short, while he has been inferring that many of our members did not read the bill, I would suggest to him that he probably does not even know the questionnaires to which he referred in his statements before this House. If the minister has not done his homework, I think it is time that I at least read into the record the type of questionnaires to which they are subjecting Canadian business at the present time.
Let me point out, Mr. Speaker, that if you took those questionnaires and hooked them up end to end you would find you have 52 feet of questionnaires every time someone has to comply with the present act. On top of that, you would have 31 feet of instructions to go along with it. That means 83 feet of paperwork for people to go through every time this act is complied with. You will recall the minister said he thought there were about 90,000 poor souls out there, not counting the labour unions, that have to comply with this type of paperwork. So if you add up all those things, you will find he is inflicting on Canadian business-and add to it the labour unions, if you like-7,470,000 feet of paper. Think of how many miles that is if it were ever stretched out.
However, let me first of all touch on what these forms are supposed to be about. The first one, questionnaire No. 1, is called "Annual Return of Corporations under the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act". This is a kind of general form dealing with a lot of information that I would suggest is relevant today in many other places, relevant I suggest in the sense that it can be found. We have a new corporations act, the provinces have corporations acts in which, in virtually every jurisdiction, the type of information solicited here is probably available under the relevant corporations act, be it provincial or federal.
The next one is the annual return of corporations called "CLR 3". This one is a more particular form but a shortened version of the larger one I referred to. We then get into two marked "confidential". I am not sure why. One is called "The Annual Report", the other is called "The Quarterly Report". Both refer to selected information on companies in Canada wholly or largely foreign owned. Probably the reason they are marked "confidential"-we would never want to disclose anything about a foreign firm here-is that this is something for the minister's eyes only, or perhaps for FIRA.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see the Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan) has joined us tonight. Undoubtedly, he has come into the House in anticipation of joining in the debate. Since this debate touches so heavily on the unions of Canada, I could never anticipate that a minister of labour would sit in this House and stay mute for an entire debate which touches upon a form which is being so opposed by the labour unions in Canada. I look forward to the Minister of Labour making a contribution later on. I hope he will be patient for I will certainly try to be brief in my remaining remarks. I only touched on a few points earlier in my speech, as you will recall, and I have a few more points I wish to make.
Just before we adjourned at dinner time I pointed out that the three questions which will now be put to Canadian businessmen, and which amount to several pages as far as forms are concerned, will, if put end to end, actually stretch to a length of 26 feet. There are 26 feet of questions which we will, in effect, allow Statistics Canada-and I see officials from StatsCan sitting in the gallery wringing their hands, wanting to get this legislation in place so they can grind out more and more forms to Canadian businessmen-to put to businessmen.
On behalf of the labour unions and corporations of Canada, and businessmen generally, we must give some protection to those sectors of our economy as far as Statistics Canada is concerned. Anyone who wishes to review the activities of that
10862

June 22, 1981
Corporations and Labour Unions
organization knows that it allows data processing and the compilation of data to run rampant if no controls are placed on it. So, I am asking that the minister reconsider this evening the actual pressing of this bill and that he reconsider whether he even wants to offer it to the House of Commons for passage in its present form. We in the official opposition believe that it may well be that the bill should be withdrawn and that studies should take place to determine whether in fact we need this legislation any longer. The type of information which is spelled out in the various drafts forms which Statistics Canada has prepared is something that, I suggest, could be obtained from other sources. At the present time in the country we have a tremendous amount of data which is already available to government. I suggest that if that date were utilized in a way that Statistics Canada desired, there would be absolutely no need to subject the businessmen and labour unions of this country to the type of documentation and form-filling which is anticipated in the bill before us tonight.
I sometimes think that the magnitude of the requirements which government places on business is overlooked. It is a formidable task which we impose on business. The total number of forms or acts, if you like, which business must comply with include the following items. There is federal sales tax collection, there is provincial sales tax collection, excise duties, customs clearance, UIC deductions, workmen's compensation, hospitalization, loan applications, building permits, equipment operating licences, property taxes, vehicle registration, transport operating licences, communication licences, income tax forms, income deductions at source, detailed house surveys, bounding, business licences, restaurants and liquor taxes, CMHC housing surveys, safety inspections, tax audits, FIRA requirements, elevator licences, boiler licences, subsidy applications, development permits, waste control, minimum wage guidelines, Statistics Canada surveys-including the type of thing we are now reviewing-manpower training programs, employee hiring procedures, government contracts procurement, grants and incentive programs, consumer protection standards, census of population, drivers' licences, welfare and health benefits, and CPI samples.
I could go on with many other things that we seem to feel we can demand of business; and yet we assume, presumably, that there is no consumer consequence or cost. The fact, as we know, is that there is a very big cost. I could mention that those various items I have read into the record were not original with me. They were items which were referred to by a minister, Tony Abbott, when he was in power as a member of this government. At that time, he was the minister for small business. He was pointing out the need to relieve small business of much of that type of requirement.
Tonight we have a golden opportunity literally to do something about this problem, which people have talked about for years and years. In short, let us consider the possibility of not amending, but simply rescinding, the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act.
Having said that, I would like to go on to point out that in the spring of 1977 an Industry, Trade and Commerce interview team went across Canada and met with business people to listen to their views on how well government operates generally, and how well industry, trade and commerce specifically operates to meet their needs. Of the 5,000 businessmen interviewed, 35 per cent identified paper burden as the major irritant they had to live with. There was no other item that the businessmen reported to that team which bothered them so much as the paper burden to which they were subjected by governments. I would suggest that that observation is consistent with the findings of the Economic Council, which recently brought in its report, indicating its concern for the impact of regulations and paper burden on small business. The council found that for small businessmen-and I use their words as a direct quote-"paperwork was the major regulatory irritant-entailing an average of one to ten hours of extra effort per week-with federal paperwork demands exceeding provincial or municipal requirements in all provinces except Quebec."
In assessing the costs exacted by government paperwork, small business can undoubtedly be singled out as particularly hard hit because small businesses do not have the resources to hire specialized personnel or outside consultants to handle the paperwork. Often, paperwork represents a direct demand on the time of the principal operator, which is time he requires to work, plan and innovate in order to stay in business and grow.
I would suggest, in that respect, that most agree today that one of the great deficiencies in our country is in the area of productivity. Our businessmen are just not producing as much as most economists would like to see them produce. Let me assure hon. members and Your Honour that the passage of this bill in its present form will put a greater load and impediment on those very businessmen to whom we are turning to get the real growth in this country going up instead of down, as far as the average worker is concerned.
The proposed amendments to the CALURA are positive in that they will exempt numerous small businesses from having to report. On that we wish to agree. I think it is good that some businesses are exempted from having to fill in the present form. However, as I indicated earlier, our question is: why do any businesses, even at a $10 million threshold level, as far as sales are concerned, or $5 million in total assets, have to live with this type of documentation and data compilation when one bears in mind that it is done at tremendous cost, not only to those businesses but, most important, to the consumers who buy from those businesses?
I would suggest to Your Honour that the government claims that 70,000 businesses will be exempted, though one wonders if this figure, first used in 1978, is still realistic given, first of all, the high interest rates resulting in many small businesses going bankrupt and discouraging others from starting up and, second, the high levels of inflation, artificially increasing sales and assets.
In short, if the minister wants to continue with this type of legislation, our feeling is that the ceiling of $10 million in sales

and $5 million in assets is too low. It was a ceiling which was first suggested in 1978. With inflation it becomes less and less as far as effective exemptions are concerned. In short, if we must have this type of legislation, let us increase the ceiling, certainly beyond the levels suggested by the minister.
For those companies which still have to report, the paperwork has been reduced, it is stated, by approximately 50 per cent. However, when one considers the over-all burden of government paperwork imposed on business, when examining CALURA one should ask the following questions: What is the purpose of the act? Has hope for benefits been measured against cost to business and government? Clearly, unless the minister misled this House, and I would hate to say that he deliberately misled the House-

Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make on Bill S-10, an act to amend the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act which is to provide for the reporting of financial and other statistics relating to the affairs of corporations and labour unions carrying on activities in Canada.
I should like to align myself with the comments made by the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) and share with the House my impression that a good many sectors of our society are opposed to this legislation. We see that it requires small unions and small businesses to be accountable in many areas, so it is obvious that they would be opposed to the legislation. To date, I have not seen the government demonstrate the need for this legislation. To my mind it is another case of government snooping or wishing to have records on practically every facet of our lives.
In its recent report, the Economic Council of Canada documented the need for deregulation rather than more regulation and reporting on that regulation. As the hon. member for York-Peel pointed out, an additional paper burden will be imposed on the small business sector. This government, as did this party when it was in power and during various election campaigns, committed itself to reducing the paper burden of the small business sector. But this legislation is another example of Liberal campaign promises being broken once it has assumed the role of government. Rather than reducing the paper burden of the productive sector of our society, the government is increasing it.
Not too long ago the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe) did away with the offices that dealt with the paper burden that had been established across Canada, so it is obvious that this government is not concerned with reducing the paper burden that had been imposed on the small business sector.
This legislation will mean that the small business sector will have to fill out even more government forms and this, in turn, will decrease business productivity. As an hon. member who spoke earlier indicated, the government has not provided any figures to show what it will cost business to do this.
In the time that I have been a member of this House, it has been obvious that the government is concerned with the redistribution of wealth rather than with the generation of wealth. This bill is another example that the government is not con-

Corporations and Labour Unions
cerned with the generation of wealth but is more than happy to place further restrictions on the business sector.
A good many members would like an opportunity to comment on this legislation and we hope they will have that opportunity when the bill is referred to committee so that there will be more feedback. I believe the legislation is worth a lengthy debate.
So much of the legislation that comes from the government attempts to structure our society so that it is aware of every move an individual makes. This is becoming a highly interventionist society because of the government's actions. It is attempting to dictate to the populace their rights and moods. We found that to be true in the wording of the constitutional proposal which indicated the government would grant certain powers to the people, rather than the reverse, that we as legislators would derive our power from the people who elect us. It is my belief that all the power and rights that we have are generated by the population.
Mr. Speaker, Jefferson said that men are naturally divided by temperament into two classes: those who fear and distrust ordinary people and want to concentrate power in the hands of a small, select elite, and those who trust and cherish ordinary people and think of them as the safest, if not always the wisest, repositories of power.
I think this illustrates the difference in the attitudes of the two major parties in this country. We have a party governing the nation that believes in the strong centralist approach; that believes that the elite few should govern and the people should do as it sees fit, rather than having input from the public at large. I am sure I speak for the majority of members on this side of the House when I indicate our belief that the Canadian people are the wisest repository of power and that we support getting more input from them.
During the constitutional debate, hon. members opposite criticized us for prolonging it. They brought in closure and choked off debate on the resolution. The excuse was that the House should be dealing with economic measures as the country was facing a severe economic situation. Mr. Speaker, the country is facing a severe economic situation and we must bring forward some measures to deal with high interest rates, but I would ask hon. members opposite where those economic measures are. The government indicated to us that when debate was completed on the constitutional resolution, it would bring economic measures forward. It has no economic measures, Mr. Speaker, to deal with the serious difficulties facing the Canadian population.
I would like to analyse the economic record of the government.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on this bill. I was shocked to see one form which will have to be filled out by businesses and labour unions as a result of passage of this bill. I hear an hon. member making a comment, but I say to him that he has looked at it, he should be shocked too. If the hon. member wants to speak on this bill, he should get on his feet and speak. That one form covers ten pages. If you take all the forms and put them end to end, they measure 26 feet. It is quite amazing. Some of the required items involving just a small businessman include purchases during the year of materials and components for manufacture and goods for resale. Many of the items will require changes to be made in the accounting systems of some companies. If this form is given to an auditor to complete, it will cost a considerable amount of money. For some time I have felt that this is really overkill. On one side of the argument we had a minister who was charged with the job of reducing the amount of paperwork which small businesses have to complete. We heard a great deal about that a couple of years ago when an hon. member was given the job. I believe the portfolio was that of minister of state for small businesses. When the hon. member left the portfolio, I asked him how many people he had in his department. Like many people in Canada I thought that the minister of state for small businesses who was in charge of reducing paperwork for small businesses would have a staff to help him. But I found out that the total establishment for that ministry consisted of the minister, two secretaries, an executive assistant and a public relations officer. Here was the minister in charge of reducing paperwork but he did not have the staff to do the job!
I recall seeing some letters that were sent out, publicity releases and copies of speeches that the minister made across the country wherein he said he would reduce the paperwork. Now we have this nonsense.
I have to relate to the House, as I have done before, an experience I had in my own business before I became involved in politics and was elected to the House of Commons. I started a small business. I had a large amount of paper coming into my office from various government agencies. I had to make a decision whether I was going to fill out the forms, as I am sure businessmen will have to do with these forms, or I was going to get on and do business to make some money to pay the bills, my staff, and so on. I took this massive pile of paper and divided it into two groups: one dealt with taxation, because we have to pay taxes, and the other was just a general information which was flowing in from Statistics Canada and other government agencies. The tax forms went to our auditor. In due course they were filed and returned to Ottawa. But the pile from the information seekers kept growing. They kept sending
Corporations and Labour Unions
more and more forms. The pile got to be quite a height until it truly reached a crisis stage in the business. I had to decide whether I was going to spend the time filling out the forms or whether I was going to make some money or do something else in the business. I decided I would dispose of this paper. I went to the rubber stamp supply house in town. I bought a large rubber stamp with the words "not applicable" on it. I bought a red stamp pad. I returned to my office and stamped all these forms "not applicable". Then I sent these forms in their envelopes back to Ottawa.
In due course I received a computerized letter which said, "we are in receipt of form number so and so, which we understand is not applicable." The letter ended with one of those squiggly signatures which look somewhat like Arabic; you cannot decipher it nor do you know who the person is. It is just a mark on a paper made by a marking instrument. I then set up a series of files with the form numbers on the tab. I placed the letter I received in answer in each one. In due course, another form came. I xeroxed the computerized letter I received from one of the government agencies which said they understood it was not applicable. I stamped the document again "not applicable", stapled it and returned it to Ottawa.
In the course of a very few months I reduced the amount of paper flow by 40 per cent. I do not think the government feels any worse about this nor do I think the affairs of the nation ground to a halt, or anything of that nature. What this did was to prove how silly and nonsensical some of these forms are. When I read through some of what my colleague calls "gob-bledygook" after looking at the census form, it makes me wonder whether we are supposed to spend our time filling out forms or doing some business. I can see to some extent the government's desire to get a handle on things as far as technology is concerned. It is concerned about the transfer of technology. The government should be trying to enhance the transfer of technology into this country. That is something we need.
In my own business in the last little while I have gone outside the country and licensed manufacturing within Canada so I would not have to import that particular product into this country. I wanted to get as high a Canadian content as possible, employ more Canadians and not contribute to the balance of payments problem. I wanted to get out of the foreign exchange hassle and so forth. I did that.
FIRA has restricted foreign investment in this country, contrary to what FIRA and government ministers will tell you. Ask the Minister of State what happens when he goes outside the country and talks about investment in Canada. He feels he must tell investors not to be afraid of FIRA.
If Canadian businesses are to be expected to sign licensing agreements or pursue patents and cross licensing with those in other countries for products or designs, we should not be discouraging them by requiring them to fill out these forms. There is a general suspicion with regard to filling out forms

when it comes to information such as the transfer of technology.
Just looking through this form, I wonder whether I will be interested in putting down the details, the information regarding my licensing agreement, the terms, how long it is for, what the product is, what category it falls into, whether the information is to be kept secret or confidential or will be available to a lot of other people.
I hope that somewhere along the line we can have another look at this matter. I would like to see it discussed at great length. I know it has been kicking around for a number of years. The Senate had a look at it. However, before we rush into this, we should have the opportunity of having the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) before us. Let him look at it along with those from Statistics Canada.
When it comes to forms, it should be the other way around. The minister and StatsCan should be required to convince an all-party committee of this House that the particular form is necessary. They should be required to come before a committee, show why it is absolutely vital that they have the form and give the reasons why. Perhaps if we had that approach, there would be a greater acceptance of the filling out of forms.
By the same token, some members of the committee will have had experience in the business sector and will have filled out such forms. People from the tax foundation, the chartered accountants' association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, people from the John Bulloch group, the Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen, and all others involved in filling out these forms should have some input. These people should be convinced through committee hearings that such and such information is absolutely vital for the government to function in the way it wants. If that were the case, there would probably be some measure of co-operation.
A tremendous amount could be gained from such a hearing. I am sure that each of these groups, organizations and individuals I have mentioned could contribute something to the construction of the form. I am sure that the same information is being collected time and time again. For example, I have run into many people who object to putting their income on the census form. They say that is their business and that of the Department of National Revenue, never the twain shall meet and there is no way they are going to put down that information. The same will be true of these forms. Businessmen have probably made quite legal arrangements with others regarding the cross licensing of technology.
I had occasion this morning to discuss with one of my colleagues a licensing arrangement with a company in Alberta. The transportation of that product to this market is too costly. It was decided to have a licensing agreement for a certain portion of the country. That company would be very reluctant to let that information become generally known across the country.

It should be withdrawn and put before an all-party committee or a task force such as the one on government regulations a while back which did a reasonably good job. That sort of approach could be taken with Bill S-10. Withdraw it and put it before an all-party committee, redraft it and bring it back here. If that approach were taken, I am sure it would receive reasonable passage through the House. The way it is now, I certainly cannot support it.

I was horrified when he did this because I thought he would be in a lot of trouble. He has never been bothered since.
I would like to hypothesize that those who absolutely ignore forms-the 12,000 strong-are those who are never bothered. Those who diligently fill out forms receive more and more forms, until they are caught in a web of forms for Ottawa. If the small business community-12,000 strong-is not filling out forms, the statistics that Statistics Canada is trying to put together must be false. They cannot be anywhere near correct. Either the government wins the support of the business community from which it is trying to gather information, it wins the support of the unions across the country from which it is trying to gather information, it shows them how it is absolutely necessary to the functioning of the government that they fill out the forms, it makes the forms simple enough so that the information can be gathered and put together very quickly, or the matter is dispensed with. You hear it time and time again, Mr. Speaker. This is the constant complaint of small business, of being inundated with form after form in the paper war, because they know they must pass that on to the consumer and they are in a competitive market out there. The government must recognize that it and Statistics Canada have lost support for the information gathering they are attempting, whether it be the census, small business, or unions. They have lost support right across the country. We are here to pass laws at the request of the voters, not to pass laws to impose on them. Too often we forget this.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberals across the way would not pause to listen for a few moments to a legitimate concern expressed to me time and again in my riding. I am sure if they sat down and read their own mail they would find they are getting the same kind of response to this continual interference in the marketplace by government. Information is gathered, statistics drawn up and shelved. Very few people need it. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been approximately Five occasions on which I felt it necessary to rise in this House to speak on bills which have created unnecessary paperwork in the business community. What is most disturbing is the fact that in all these debates that I can think of the minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) has not been present to give at least some measure of support to the opposition parties as they put forth their thoughts in this regard.
I recognize, Mr. Speaker, that there have been four recent attempts to amend CALURA. It was passed first in 1962 to allow collection of financial and other information on certain corporations and labour unions operating in Canada. It was amended once in 1965. What has happened in recent years is that the government has made several attempts to amend the act, first, with Bill C-7 in the third session of the Thirtieth Parliament; second, with Bill C-3, in the fourth session of the Thirtieth Parliament; third, with Bill C-12, in the first session of the Thirty-first Parliament; and finally, with Bill S-10 in the first session of the Thirty-second Parliament.
In presenting Bill C-7 to the House, the minister of State for small businesses gave three main reasons why the amendment of CALURA was necessary. He said that since 1962:
-the economy has become much more complex and policymakers, as a consequence, have had to request additional date to keep abreast of developments.
His second reason was:
At present, over 90,000 corporations file ownership schedules under the act. The majority of these respondents are small, Canadian, privately owned businesses, originally not intended to be under the purview of the act. Bill C-7 is expected to relieve some 70,000 of these businesses from reporting under the act.
So said the minister in referring to Bill C-7. The third reason was:
As part of a streamlining process, Bill C-7 integrates six Statistics Canada questionnaires and two questionnaires collected by Industry, Trade and Commerce into one single questionnaire.
One significant new amendment has to do with trans-border technology transfers, and I will refer to that in just a moment. Let us take a look at returns filed by corporations under part one of CALURA as of June 15, 1978. We must bear in mind that there are many parts and many forms, some of them as long as seven pages, to be filled out, but let us just take a look at part one. It is somewhat shocking to learn, going back to 1974, that 77,869 businesses were filing. In 1975 it went up to 94,562. For the date year 1976, in which more than 85,000 filed, collection this year is still in progress.
The number of corporation returns outstanding is shocking. Let us take a look for a minute at how the business community reacts to CALURA and at some of the businesses which ignore the forms. Let us discuss statistics to see how we stand. We will deal with 1974 and 1975, because the government is still collecting the outstanding forms for 1976.
In 1974 a total of 1,610 businesses never filed, refused to file. What has the government done to those businesses in relation to the 77,000 businesses which took the time to fill out
June 22, 1981

this multitude of paperwork? To my knowledge, the government has done nothing. For data year 1975, there are 1,517 businesses that have not filed as yet. For the data year 1976, collection is still in progress. It is estimated that returns from approximately 12,000 corporations are yet to be received. Of those, 124 corporations with assets of over $5 million have yet to file.
I should like to deal with the burden imposed by CALURA on businesses. The present situation is that there are eight questionnaires. There are 52 feet of questions and 31 feet of instructions, if the paper is measured lengthwise. On an annual basis, there are 83 feet of paperwork for a corporation. For the
90,000	businesses operating in Canada, times the 83 feet, there are 7,470,000 feet of paperwork. This is the same government that told Canadians if it was elected it would reduce the paper load on behalf of small business.
On an annual basis, government personnel handle 52 feet times 90,000 or 4,680,000 feet of paperwork to process CALURA questionnaires returned by businesses in Canada. This does not include the paperwork generated by CALURA questionnaires which are sent to unions. We would have to add that amount to the list as well.
I should like to give a few figures relating to the costs associated with personnel in the administration of CALURA. What is it costing the taxpayers of Canada to administer CALURA in Ottawa in this massive government bureaucracy? Under an amended CALURA, there are three questionnaires which I have. There are 26 feet of questions and a small number of instructions. With only 20,000 businesses reporting, the paperwork generated would be 520,000 feet. This is still a considerable sum when one takes into account all the paperwork businesses have imposed upon them by governments today. What does it cost Ottawa to administer CALURA?
I should like to indicate three basic examples in man-years. In Ottawa, 43.5 man-years were spent in the 1977-78 fiscal year to administer the corporation area of CALURA. What did that cost? In the one fiscal year of 1977-78, the cost to administer the corporation branch was $843,000. To administer the labour unions area, there were eight man-years at a cost of $128,000. To administer CALURA alone, it took 2.5 man-years at a cost of $87,000. What business would not consider it a plum to be handed $87,000 in return for 2.5 man-years? In 1977-78 it took a total of 54 man-years to administer CALURA at a cost of $1,058,000.
Who is featherbedding? Who is gaining advantage from CALURA today? It is certainly not the business community. I do not see the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism standing in the House and asking the government to show some compassion and consideration for the small business community.
This is only one more bill in a great number of pieces of legislation which have brought extreme costs to bear upon the Canadian business community. These costs are passed on to consumers, thus inflation is inflamed and our ever-growing cost of living is increased.
Corporations and Labour Unions
CALURA represents only a small portion of the over-all paperwork imposed upon businesses by governments at all levels in Canada today-municipal, provincial and federal. We are specifically discussing federal in this Parliament. We are asking the government to live up to its commitment to the small business community and to show some tangible evidence of its concern and interest in reducing the paper burden upon the small business community.
Paper burden is defined as information requirements established by government which can be judged to be unduly burdensome and very costly. They include application forms, reports, surveys, record-keeping requirements, and unnecessarily complex regulations and procedures. At the federal level numerous acts and their attendant provisions, procedures, standards, etc., all impose paperwork over and above the call of duty upon the small business community.
There are 16 departments and agencies-the Department of Agriculture, CMHC, CCA, CRTC, CTC, DREE, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, Environment Canada, the Department of Health and Welfare, the Department of Labour, Revenue Canada, Statistics Canada, The Department of Supply and Services, to name but a few. When will we receive some tangible evidence that the government is sincere in its intent to reduce paperwork?
In addition to federal department and agencies, provincial, regional and municipal programs generate massive amounts of paperwork upon the business community today. That is the reason there are 6,000 or 7,000 bankruptcies annually in the small business sector. This figure is growing on a monthly basis. This is one of the major reasons for small business bankruptcies. A one or two-person operation requires almost an equal number of staff to administer its operations today to keep up with the burden of paperwork. The magnitude of these requirements is formidable, as the following list of required government paperwork illustrates.
I have a list of 45 government agencies that all require reports to be filled out by the business community. We must give credit where credit is due-there are some exceptions, but by and large very little compassion is shown for the business community. Meeting these paperwork requirements imposes a significant cost upon the public as well as the private sector, but these costs have not been accurately tabulated in Canada. One United States estimates puts the annual dollar cost for federal government paperwork at $500 for each United States citizen. First there are the economic costs which vary from business to business, from person to person. They include the time cost to design, develop and instal information systems in businesses; direct and indirect costs of data collection; the costs of processing and analysis, filling out forms, hiring consultants, lawyers and accountants. What small incorporated business can operate today without the services of one or two chartered accountants? I suggest, Mr. Speaker, very few. It was not many years ago that a small businessman, an entrepreneur who wanted to open up a business, could do his paperwork in the evenings in an hour or two. I defy him to do

June 22, 1981
Corporations and Labour Unions that today. Even operating a business as basic as a service station requires countless reams of paper to be filled out for government agencies, both provincial and federal. This government has very little compassion for the small business community.
These costs are more difficult to measure, but they exist and are expressed in terms of anger and frustration, disillusionment and helplessness. Helplessness because they feel they have been betrayed by governments which made the solemn promise that they would reduce paperwork, show that they care and that there would be some action. And what do we do in this House of Commons week after week? We come in here and debate legislation which will put greater pressure on the strength of our country, the free enterprise system. Very seldom do we see a ray of light in this House of Commons to the point where we would conscientiously reduce the load we are bringing to bear on the business sector of our society which offers us a degree of hope in the future.
In the spring of 1977 the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce interview teams went across Canada and met with business people to hear their views on how well government operates generally and, specifically, how well IT&C operates to meet the needs of the business community. Of the
5,000	businessmen interviewed, 35 per cent identified paper burden as the major irritant. Who sits in this House today who did not campaign in 1979 and again in 1980 with the solemn promise to decrease that paper burden borne by the business community? I will agree that there are only some 47 people here on the other side of the House who know what it is like to be in business today. I doubt if there are even that many. But I know 47 businessmen who sit in this House of Commons. They said they would reduce paperwok. What we spend most of our time doing in this House is adding to the paperwork of the small business sector. This is consistent with the findings of the Economic Council of Canada in its concern for the impact of regulations and paper burden on small business.
Let us take a look at what the Economic Council of Canada said. The Council found that for small businessmen:
-paperwork was the major regulatory irritant-entailing an average of one to ten hours of extra effort per week-with federal paperwork demands exceeding provincial or municipal requirements in all provinces except Quebec.
Some credit may be given to the Quebec provincial government but no credit is due to the 75 members who sit in this House from the province of Quebec. The Economic Council says that this Liberal government has been remiss in its promise to the people to reduce the paper load.
In assessing costs exacted by government paperwork, small business can undoubtedly be singled out as particularly hard hit, because small businesses do not have the resources to hire specialized personnel or outside consultants to handle the paperwork. Paperwork often represents a direct demand on the time of the principal operator, the time he requires to work, to plan and to be productive. Why do we on this Hill have less than 60 per cent productivity? It is because the government
does not know how to manage its own shop. Until we manage our own shop better and until we start doing the kinds of things we said we would do when the people elected us, we will not change the situation. It is no wonder that to a large degree the people of Canada have lost faith in governments today. I do not know of one of the five promises made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in January, 1980, that has been kept. That is why the business community has lost faith in Parliament, because it did not do what it said it would do when it campaigned in the 1980 election-

The proposed amendments to CALURA are positive-this is what the Council says-in that they will exempt numerous small businesses from having to report. That is a lot of hogwash. There are 1,817 businesses which have not reported since 1976 anyway. In other words, in 1976 there were 75,000 businesses which should not have taken the time to fill out these 38 pages or 90,000 feet of paperwork.
June 22, 1981

This government is making fools out of the business community in Canada today. The government claims that 70,000 businesses will be exempted. In 1974 only 77,000 reported, and now this government is going to exempt 70,000? Who are the remainder? Are we going through this two days of debate to make 7,000 business people fill out all this paperwork and hire a bureaucracy, which will cost us a million dollars this year, to administer this act in Ottawa? The figures do not add up, Mr. Speaker. The small business community is receiving another snow job.
For those companies which still have to report the paperwork has been reduced by approximately 50 per cent. This is what the government says. What does that mean? According to the statistics, of the 7,000 which still have to report, only 3,500 will actually report. Or does it mean that the 7,000 will do half as much? If that is so, then I ask the government by how much it will reduce the bureaucracy to administer this program. Is the government going to reduce the staff which administers CALURA by 50 per cent? Not a chance. There is no sunset clause in this government. The expenses will go on as usual. Even if we agree with the objectives of CALURA and even if we agree that in order for the government to operate today it requires more statistics, we must be concerned about the government's use of the information collected.
This bill, before it is passed, should go before a group of people, namely, one headed by the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism. The minister, whose job it is to look after the business community, should appoint an all-party committee to scrutinize CALURA to report to the business community. Through whatever organizations it would like to report to, whether it is the Canadian Organization of Small Business or the Federation of Independent Business, it should report to them and justify the bill before it is passed. The bill should not be brought into this House and then shoved through under the guise that the government's taking the interest of the small businessman and the reduction of his paper load into consideration.
In recent years the Liberal governments have tried to exert more and more control through legislation, regulation and industrial development programs. We have seen it in the budget, we have seen it in the energy policy and we have seen it in the Constitution. The information provided by these businesses through CALURA will undoubtedly be used by this government to continue in this vein of gathering information for ulterior motives. It is sad to see this bill going through the House, with speaker after speaker from the Conservative party here speaking on behalf of a small business community and very little action from anywhere else. I think that any time we introduce paperwork into this House we are betraying the people who we campaigned to support if we were elected. We are showing a complete disregard for our election commitments to reduce paperwork by the setting up of offices to scrutinize and justify the paperwork before it is imposed upon the business community.
Corporations and Labour Unions
One of my colleagues has already pointed out to this House that those offices which were set up to scrutinize paperwork and to show that it was necessary before the legislation was implemented, are no longer in place. Why has this government presented this piece of legislation without first showing the business community that it was necessary and that there were offshoots from which would benefit the people who are most adversely affected by this paperwork? There is every reason in the world why we as a government and as a Parliament should oppose this bill, Bill S-10, as it appears now for second reading debate as amendments to CALURA.
