Mr. Speaker, I have been listening to the debate. I am glad to see that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan) is in the House this evening. I want to speak to him briefly through Your Honour. I do not know whether he is aware of the impact of this bill upon those parts of the economy which fall under his partial jurisdiction in the House of Commons, in terms of reporting at least at the federal level. I am talking about labour unions. I think he has been here during two periods of the debate in the House. I was rather hoping he would inject himself into the debate with respect to this matter. I still remain with the hope that there will be time for him to do that. My understanding of the matter goes back some distance to the days when I was practising law and acting for national associations. I had concern then, and I still have that concern, with respect to the kind of information which is being requested.
Thus far the debate has focused on the impact of this legislation, particularly as it relates to difficulties of people who happen to be incorporated and engaged in small business, people who run the businesses by themselves and for whom accountancy help and legal help is a major overhead factor.
Viewing a bill such as this, which now requires the filling of some eight rather complicated forms, one could wonder if the government is doing anything other than lessening appreciably not only the number of forms, but also the kinds of businesses to which those forms apply. What has really happened is that instead of a member of a business being able to choose the kind of form which applies to the particular business in question, now everyone who happens to be in a small business must fill out all these forms, whether or not they are relevant to the kind of business being carried out. The government may have lessened the weight of the paper; but rather than lessening the onerous duty upon the small businesses to fill out forms, the filing has been made much more broad so that they apply to a larger number of businesses. Therefore, every business must fill out one of these forms whether or not that particular matter applies to them.
If the government will think about it for a moment, it will find that it has compounded the problems of the small businessmen with respect to filing. This is the first point I would like to make.
Second, I wonder if there has, in fact, been any consultation with the small business sector. Each one of us in this House

June 22, 1981
Corporations and Labour Unions
receives correspondence each month from the members of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business who are largely small business people trying to make their way in a world which is tough enough as it is without also having to deal with paper. Was a consultative group ever established by the government to talk to such a group of representative businessmen-and there may be others in the community-to see whether this is really necessary or whether there is another way that this information, which is admittedly important to government, could be made available so that government would have it at its fingertips? I daresay that if the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) were to check the records, he would find that there has been very little consultation at all with the small business sector. There is no reason at all to worry too much about the multinational corporations, but one must be concerned about that. If there were some further consultation, having regard to the debate which has taken place in this House, it might lessen the burden on business. I hope that the minister will undertake to continue that discussion before this bill gets through.
The other matter I want to refer to now is the question of the information which is required in the forms themselves. By the way, Your Honour knows this is information which is filed with the government in confidence so that the government can plan. If that is the case-and I have no reason to doubt that- then it seems to me that it is the kind of information which is perhaps already within the knowledge of the government. Corporate information which is filed relating to directors' shareholdings and things of that nature is the kind of information which could be incorporated into and form part of government information. In fact, a great deal of it could be gleaned from the returns which are now filed annually with the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs from corporations and incorporated businesses, and that would cut down some of the duplication.
Another aspect which the government should perhaps consider, and may consider on second thought, is the availability of information within the Department of National Revenue. I happen to know that the Department of National Revenue is scrupulous in preserving the confidentiality of information filed with it by taxpayers. However, I daresay that if one would put the alternative of filing a form like this to any businessman, or allowing another department to consult with the Department of National Revenue on the basis of confidence, and if a waiver were signed to that effect, and if that businessman could be assured that he would not have to fill out one other form or deal with another pile of papers at the same time as he is trying to sell, I am sure that that businessman would opt for the simpler method of granting the waiver on the understanding, of course, that it would be confidential.
I think this would go a long way toward reducing the amount of paper that the small business community has to deal with and about which it is always cursing governments.
Governments have made great strides, Mr. Speaker. When I was minister of national revenue I gave credit to officials of
the department for streamlining import procedures on the customs side of the operation, so that people did not have to file for each transaction but could file over a longer period of time and thus facilitate matters.
Within government itself there is a desire to cut down on the number of filings that are necessary, although many people do not believe this to be the case. If it would take advantage of the expertise that is available in the public service, it could do a great deal in this direction, but sometimes I think it does not realize this. The business life of the small businessman could be relieved of further complications if, for instance, he did not have to file an international trade form when he is not engaged in international trade. The system, which was complicated enough before, has become more complicated, and I think it could be changed.
The government ought to be given an opportunity to reconsider this bill, Mr. Speaker. It is not urgent. I suggest it withdraw the bill and consult with the business community to see whether, by marrying the expertise that there is in the private sector with that in the public sector, something more relevant, not just for government, but for small business, could be devised.
I am not going to carry the debate any further, Mr. Speaker, except to say that I think the government ought to consider withdrawing the bill and dealing with the question in another way. We would be happy to assist it in that undertaking.
I hope this view is shared by members on the other side, although sometimes I have my doubts-that the small businessman ought to be burdened as little as possible. He is overloaded with paperwork as things stand now. I am sure there is not one member of the House who does not have a constituent who complains about the amount of filing that has to be done to government. I think we ought to be attempting to lessen this instead of increasing it.
